### Secrets vault [page: secrets-vault]

Five tools handle credentials, and two more type them into web pages. These seven tools keep plaintext out of their arguments and results: the model gets a reference, and SoAI does the typing.

This page covers the tool workflow and storage details. [Passwords and credential tools](#passwords-and-credential-tools) explains how this boundary differs from WebUI passwords and generated strings, and what remains at risk after a credential is protected from the model.

In the SoAI WebUI, make a vault tool available by selecting **Chat configuration** in the chat header, then **Tools**. Turn on **Tools enabled**, choose the tool for the required mode, and select **Save**. The account needs **MCP usage** ([`MCP_USE`](#acl-MCP_USE)) and the selected model must support tool calling. **Credential collection and browser autofill normally require the authenticated SoAI WebUI because the dialog is where the secret is entered.** A messaging account can allow a plaintext provider reply for a vault credential request, but that option has a different security boundary described below.

#### Credentials in chat

An agent could use `ask_user` to ask for a password, and the answer would land in the conversation. From there it goes into the prompt on every following turn, into the stored transcript, into any export of that conversation, and out to the model provider if the model is remote. **A password pasted into a chat is a password you have to change.**

The vault tools break that chain. You type the credential into a SoAI dialog, SoAI keeps it, and the model receives an opaque handle. The handle is useless to anything except a later SoAI tool call.

#### Collecting a credential

Two tools open the prompt, and they differ in what they are for.

| Tool | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `vault_login_request` | A website login, tied to a `url`. Offers to save, and takes a `label_suggestion` for the saved entry. Flagged for approval. |
| `vault_secret_request` | Any credential, with a custom `title` and `message`. Saving to the vault is offered by default; a call can set `allow_save_to_vault: false` to remove that option. |

Either way a dialog appears in the chat with **Username** and **Password** fields, a **Label**, and a **Save this credential** checkbox when saving is on offer. Ticking it requires a label, since that is how you will recognise the entry later. **Submit** sends it, **Cancel** refuses, and the agent is told which happened without learning anything else.

What comes back to the model is a `secret_handle`: a random token that names the credential without revealing it. SoAI keeps handles in memory for ten minutes and enforces caps of 200 per user and 5,000 across the installation. Creating too many evicts the oldest handles. A handle from one conversation does not work in another. **A successful `browser_autofill_secret` call consumes its handle, so the agent must request a new one before another fill.**

##### Credential requests in messaging conversations

When an agent in a [Discord](https://discord.com/), [Telegram](https://telegram.org/), or [WhatsApp](https://www.whatsapp.com/) conversation requests a credential, SoAI sends a secure link to the matching conversation in the authenticated Chat page. Secret questions use the same secure path. The link requires an HTTPS [`SERVER.PUBLIC_ORIGIN`](#config-SERVER.PUBLIC_ORIGIN) that the signed-in owner of the messaging account can reach. It can remain private behind a local network or VPN; the messaging provider does not open this link. The owner opens it and completes the secure prompt in Chat.

The messaging account option **Allow plaintext secret replies** applies only to vault credential requests (not ordinary secret questions). When it is on, the remote user may reply with the credential in the provider conversation. SoAI does not save that plaintext reply to the vault, but the provider may retain it in message history, notifications, or its own systems. **Keep the option off when the secure Chat link is available.** See [Connect messaging apps to SoAI](#connect-messaging-apps-to-soai) for messaging account settings and remote interaction replies.

The caps come from [`TOOLS.MCP.SECRET_PROMPT.HANDLE_STORE_MAX_PER_USER`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SECRET_PROMPT.HANDLE_STORE_MAX_PER_USER) and [`TOOLS.MCP.SECRET_PROMPT.HANDLE_STORE_MAX_TOTAL`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SECRET_PROMPT.HANDLE_STORE_MAX_TOTAL). To change them, an administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) selects **Open settings menu** at the right of the header, then **Settings**. Select **Advanced** in the Settings page header. The page becomes **Advanced settings** and the control changes to **Basic**. Search for the key, edit it, and select **Save**.

#### Vault storage

SoAI encrypts saved credentials with [Fernet](https://cryptography.io/) before writing them to the database. The key file comes from [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_ENCRYPTION_KEY`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_ENCRYPTION_KEY), and SoAI resolves a relative value under [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA). The default path is `data/secret.key`.

The file can contain several [Fernet](https://cryptography.io/) keys, one nonempty key per line. SoAI encrypts new values with the first key and tries every listed key while decrypting. SoAI has no WebUI rotation control and does not rewrite existing vault rows automatically. A staged rotation therefore keeps older keys in the file until no stored value depends on them; removing one earlier makes those values unreadable.

**Back that key up separately from the database.** A database backup without the key is a file of unrecoverable ciphertext, and there is no recovery path: nobody can decrypt those entries, including you.

To clear everything, the signed-in user selects **Open settings menu** at the right of the header, then **Settings** and **Reset**, and uses **Password manager**. It deletes every saved credential for the signed-in account and invalidates that account's live handles. There is no undo.

#### Reading the vault

`vault_list` lists saved credentials and `vault_search` finds them by label. **Both return metadata only: labels, identifiers, and dates, never a password.** That is enough for an agent to say *I have a saved login for that site* and to pass the right ID to an autofill tool.

`vault_delete` removes one by `credential_id`. It is destructive and flagged for approval, so Plan mode refuses it and you get asked first.

#### Filling in a login

Two browser tools do the typing, and neither one receives the secret as an argument.

- `browser_autofill_secret` uses a `secret_handle` from one of the request tools, for a credential you entered for this task.
- `browser_autofill_vault` uses a `credential_id` from the vault, for one saved earlier.

Both take the page `url`, optional `username_ref` and `password_ref` pointing at the fields from a browser snapshot, and `submit` to press the login button afterwards. Leave the refs out and SoAI finds the username and password fields itself, which is usually right and occasionally is not. On a page with several forms, pass the refs.

`browser_navigate` can also use a `secret_handle` for HTTP Basic Auth. It consumes the handle when it resolves the credentials for that navigation.

The request tools bind each credential to the collection URL's origin. Before autofill, SoAI compares the target's scheme, IDNA-canonical hostname, and explicitly written port. A lookalike domain, another scheme, or a different port does not match.

**SoAI stores approval for these two tools per origin rather than per tool.** Approving a fill on one site does not approve it anywhere else. When SoAI cannot determine the origin from the arguments, it asks every time and stores nothing.

#### Protection boundary

The vault path keeps secrets out of the prompt, transcript, and request/autofill tool arguments and results. It encrypts them at rest and prevents the autofill tools from typing them into a different origin.

**This protection applies to the vault and autofill path, not to every browser capability.** The default-enabled `browser_eval` tool can run arbitrary JavaScript in the page and can read a filled password field while its value remains in the DOM. Disable [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED) and leave `browser_eval` out of the selected tools when the model must not be able to retrieve a filled credential.

Approval authorizes the agent to use the credential. After login, every browser tool in that session can act as the account. Anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key can decrypt saved credentials. The destination site and its scripts receive the submitted credential and control what happens after login.

Treat approving an autofill as handing over the account for the rest of that session, and see [Browser automation tools](#browser-automation-tools) for what that session can then do.

## Operating

### Administration overview [page: administration-overview]

Use the SoAI WebUI for everyday administration: first setup, accounts, backups, network access, and operational checks. Use the [HTTP API reference](#http-api-reference) when you need to automate the same operations.

#### Set up administration and access

A new installation has no accounts. Open the WebUI and complete the setup wizard to create the first administrator. Until that step finishes, authenticated application routes return `setup_required` and the WebUI continues to show the wizard. The first account becomes an administrator automatically.

##### Manage users and permissions

An administrator whose ACL grants **User administration** ([`USER_ADMIN`](#acl-USER_ADMIN)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then selects **Settings** from its menu. Open **Users** and select **Create user**. Enter the account details, then choose **Administrator** or **Regular user** in the role prompt. Administrators receive the administrative access policy; regular users can use only the actions granted to them.

**ACL policy applies actions to roles, not individual accounts.** Before changing a role-wide permission or promoting an account, read [Access control](#access-control) for the WebUI workflow, defaults, fixed actions, and complete permission table.

#### Protect and expose the instance

An administrator whose ACL grants **Backup administration** ([`BACKUP_ADMIN`](#acl-BACKUP_ADMIN)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then selects **Settings** from its menu. Open **Backup** and select **Create backup**. After it completes as valid, select **Verify**. Valid backups also enable **Restore**; every listed backup has **Download** and **Delete** unless another backup operation is running. Treat **Restore** as a recovery operation: read the restore confirmation and the [Restore](#restore) guide before applying it to a working instance.

Backups run every 24 hours by default and retain up to seven backups for up to 720 hours. By default, the enabled targets are the database, core configuration, encryption key, plugin configuration, user data, and GPU settings. User data covers the configured files and wallpaper storage. Logs are **not** a default backup target; enable [`DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.LOGS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.LOGS) if you need them in a backup. **Models and backend runtimes are not backup targets.**

The backup process records its selected targets in a manifest and checks [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) integrity before treating a database backup as complete. Review the [Backup](#backup) page for target configuration, retention, and a recovery checklist.

##### Network access and reverse proxies

The main API listens on port `5090` by default. Change it with [`SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.PORT`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.PORT). SoAI also uses the discovery range `7950` through `7960` so the WebUI can find a non-default API port during startup.

No browser origins are allowed cross-origin by default: [`SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOWED_ORIGINS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOWED_ORIGINS) starts as an empty list. Add only the exact browser origins that need cross-origin access. If SoAI runs behind a reverse proxy, forward WebSocket upgrade traffic. **The WebUI uses its WebSocket connection for live state and does not fall back to polling when that connection is unavailable.** See [Network and TLS](#network-and-tls) for TLS, public origins, and proxy headers.

#### Monitor health and control the lifecycle

Use **Metrics** in the sidebar and **Logs** in the **Settings** menu at the right of the header for routine diagnosis. Logs can also be added to the sidebar from **Settings > Theme > Sidebar**: at **Visible pages**, select **Edit**, enable **Logs**, then select **Save**. The configured application log location is controlled by [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH). The audit log records security-relevant operations such as sign-in activity, API-key changes, and terminal session lifecycle events.

For a plugin that fails to start or becomes unavailable, check its status in **Plugins** first, then review its logs and the failure model in [Resilience and self-healing](#resilience-and-self-healing). Follow [Reset an open circuit](#recover-an-unavailable-plugin) or [Make a quarantined plugin available again](#make-a-quarantined-plugin-available-again), depending on the state. Avoid resetting the whole instance to resolve an isolated plugin problem.

### Monitoring and observability [page: monitoring-and-observability]

Use the SoAI WebUI to check SoAI's state, workload, hardware, and logs. The monitoring pages draw from the same live services, but each one answers a different operational question. Use the [HTTP API reference](#http-api-reference) when a script needs the compatible client APIs or the System API.

#### Choose a monitoring page

| Page | Use it for | Access condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dashboard** | Instance status, request activity, plugins, models, hardware, network, storage, logs, and other configurable overview cards. | **System status access** ([`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ)) opens the page. Cards backed by protected resources also require their own access, including [`MODEL_READ`](#acl-MODEL_READ), [`PLUGIN_READ`](#acl-PLUGIN_READ), [`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ), or [`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS) as applicable. |
| [**Hardware**](#hardware-monitoring) | Current CPU, memory, storage, network, and GPU data, stored hardware history, export, and supported host controls. | **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)). Process information requires [`HW_PROCESS_VIEW`](#acl-HW_PROCESS_VIEW), while GPU changes require [`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING). |
| **Metrics** | Request, latency, token, queue, plugin, model, system, and frontend telemetry. | Any signed-in account. **API key usage** appears only for an Administrator and requires [`OPENAI_API_ADMIN`](#acl-OPENAI_API_ADMIN). |
| **Logs** | Current SoAI Core and available plugin log streams. | **Log access** ([`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS)) |

A **Regular user** account does not receive [`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ) or [`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ) by default, although an Administrator with [`ACL_ADMIN`](#acl-ACL_ADMIN) can grant either action to the **Standard user** ACL group. In the WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, select **Settings**, then **ACL**, expand **Standard user** in **Access control policy**, enable the required action, and select **Save**. [`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS), [`HW_PROCESS_VIEW`](#acl-HW_PROCESS_VIEW), and [`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING) remain administrator-only actions. See [Access control](#access-control) for the full access policy.

#### Use the monitoring pages

##### Dashboard

Open **Dashboard** from the side navigation for a broad view of the instance. Its movable sections can include **Status**, **Requests**, **Plugins**, **Models**, **Hardware widgets**, **Network**, **Storage**, **Logs**, **Image**, **Memo**, **Clock**, **Throughput**, and **Quick actions**. SoAI OS also adds **Capabilities** for host-level capability checks. [`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ) grants access to Dashboard but does not override the permission required by an individual card, so a user may open the page without seeing every protected card.

Select **Edit layout** in the page header to rearrange or hide sections. Hardware and Metrics use the same layout control. To disable layout editing, select **Settings**, **Theme**, **Dashboard**, then enable **Lock layouts**.

Open **Plugins** when a card identifies a problem with one backend or circuit, and open **Models** when the problem is limited to a model. Use [Operational runbooks](#operational-runbooks) for recovery procedures after you identify the affected resource.

##### Hardware

1. Open **Hardware** from the side navigation.
2. Review the CPU, memory, storage, network, and GPU data reported by the host.
3. In **Chart**, choose **Device** and **Metric**, then select a chart type and time range.

An OHLC chart also provides **Interval** for its time buckets. The page shows **History is disabled by the backend.** when history collection is off, while the values and controls that appear depend on the detected device, driver, and vendor tooling. Continue with [Hardware monitoring](#hardware-monitoring) for chart, history, and export details, or [GPU setup and troubleshooting](#gpu-setup-and-troubleshooting) when telemetry or controls are missing.

**GPU control** appears only for an account with [`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING). It shows **No GPU controls available** when no detected GPU reports an actionable control; otherwise each panel contains only the controls supported by that GPU. Read [GPU controls and tuning](#gpu-controls-and-tuning) before changing power, clocks, fan settings, or saved slots.

##### Metrics

Open **Metrics** from the side navigation. In **Chart**, select **Requests**, **Latency**, **Tokens**, or **Queue depth**, then choose the chart type and time range. **Request distribution**, **Plugin usage**, **Model usage**, **System performance**, and **Frontend telemetry** provide more focused views, while **More** opens **Advanced metrics**. **API key usage** appears only for an Administrator, and loading its data also requires [`OPENAI_API_ADMIN`](#acl-OPENAI_API_ADMIN).

Select **Export** to open a preview, then download the metrics-history CSV. Available history intervals and the metrics stored in history come from the server's current metrics configuration.

##### Logs

1. Open **Logs** from the **Settings** button at the right of the header. If Logs has been added to the sidebar, that link opens the same page.
2. Select **Core** or an available plugin source.
3. Choose the number of visible entries, then use **Increase text size** or **Decrease text size** if needed.

The visible-line choices are 100, 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 5,000. With no saved preference, the page defaults to 250 lines, and the browser remembers the selected source and line count. **Clear** empties the browser view but does not delete a log file, and new stream entries continue to arrive. The page follows incoming entries while you remain at the bottom of the view. If server logging is disabled, no log sources are available.

The main log directory and file name come from [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH) and [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG). By default, SoAI rotates the main log daily at local midnight, retains 5 rotated files, and leaves compression off. The settings are [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG_BACKUP_COUNT`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG_BACKUP_COUNT) and [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGGING_SYSTEM.MAIN_LOG_COMPRESS_LOGS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGGING_SYSTEM.MAIN_LOG_COMPRESS_LOGS).

#### Connection freshness and recovery

Live monitoring uses the authenticated WebSocket at `/api/v1/system/ws`, with no polling fallback. During a disconnect or recovery, the WebUI can retain the last valid snapshot while its connection state changes and it requests fresh data. **Treat retained values as last-known state, not current state, until an update arrives.** Logs shows **Reconnecting to log stream...** while its stream reconnects.

If live data does not recover, check the browser's WebSocket connection and any proxy or firewall that handles the WebUI connection. Use [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) for the WebUI and real-time diagnostic checks.

#### Sampling, history, and retention

To change these settings, an Administrator with [`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, selects **Settings**, then **Advanced**. Metrics and logging settings are under **Observability**, while hardware collection is under **System** and **Hardware**. Select **Save** after an edit, then select **Restart SoAI** when the WebUI reports that the change requires a restart.

| Collection | Factory default | Configuration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware collection and history | Sampled every 3 seconds, history enabled, retained for 168 hours | [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS), [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED), and [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DB_RETENTION_HOURS`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DB_RETENTION_HOURS) |
| Metrics broadcasts to the WebUI | Every 1 second | [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.BROADCAST_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.BROADCAST_INTERVAL_MS) |
| Metrics history | Enabled, sampled every 3 seconds, retained for 168 hours. The configured result limit is 50,000 points. The WebUI uses WebSocket snapshots and respects that configured limit, while the REST history endpoint accepts a `points` parameter of at most 25,000. | [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.ENABLED`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.ENABLED), [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.LOGGING_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.LOGGING_INTERVAL_MS), [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.DB_RETENTION_HOURS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.DB_RETENTION_HOURS), [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.MAX_POINTS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.MAX_POINTS), [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.SUPPORTED_INTERVALS_MS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.SUPPORTED_INTERVALS_MS), and [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.TRACKED_METRICS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.TRACKED_METRICS) |

**Live broadcasts and stored history are independent, so disabling metrics history does not stop current Metrics updates.** An empty [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.TRACKED_METRICS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.TRACKED_METRICS) list uses SoAI's built-in history set for total, completed, and failed requests, generated tokens, and queue size.

### Resilience and self-healing [page: resilience-and-self-healing]

SoAI stays usable under load and during failures because it refuses to hold more work than it can finish, and because every accepted request exists as a durable record before anything schedules it. Failures stay where they happen: a dispatch circuit stops new work from reaching a failing plugin, while the Plugin Guardian watches runtime health and performs bounded recovery. The WebUI reports those two states separately, since either one can make a plugin unavailable for a different reason.

#### Admission under load

An inference request becomes a durable task and queue item in the database before the scheduler ever sees it, which is what lets accepted work outlive a crash or a restart. Acceptance can also fail, and it fails before SoAI takes responsibility for the request: free space below [`MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT) returns a disk-space error, and a positive [`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS) that the durable queue has already reached returns a capacity error.

Past acceptance the request enters a bounded in-memory priority queue. When that queue is full a new request waits up to 10 seconds for a slot, and if none frees in that window SoAI answers 503 Service Unavailable with a queue-full error, marked transient so a client that retries on transient failures can send it again. That 10-second admission wait is fixed and not configurable. Either outcome is explicit, so a request holds a durable record or it received a refusal it can act on.

**Reaching the queue is not the same as running.** SoAI limits how many local backends run at once, how many tasks one plugin runs in parallel, and how many tasks one owner can have running, where an owner is an account, an automation, or an API key, so a single heavy client cannot occupy every slot. Waiting requests gain priority as they age, after 25 seconds for standard requests ([`MODELS.ROUTING.STANDARD_PRIORITY_AGING_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.STANDARD_PRIORITY_AGING_SEC)) and 120 seconds for flex requests ([`MODELS.ROUTING.FLEX_PRIORITY_AGING_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.FLEX_PRIORITY_AGING_SEC)), which keeps low-priority work from starving behind a steady stream of higher-priority traffic. [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning) holds the controls and their factory values, and [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) covers choosing them for a workload.

SoAI has been tested through bursts of thousands of simultaneous requests across one plugin and across several, and the instance stays available and usable: the WebUI keeps responding, accepted work keeps reaching a terminal state, and requests beyond the admission limits receive a capacity error rather than an unbounded wait. Longer request timeouts let more queued requests finish when the workload justifies them. A queue absorbs a burst and does not add capacity, so size the deployment for completed throughput rather than for queue depth.

#### Retries and rerouting

An attempt that fails for a reason the retry policy treats as transient, such as a transport error or an upstream 5xx, is retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff that starts at 1 second, grows to a 30-second ceiling, and carries jitter so retries from concurrent requests do not land together. A provider that answers 429 gets a longer budget of 10 attempts, and SoAI honors the `Retry-After` header when the provider sends one, still capped at 30 seconds per wait. **A failure the policy does not classify as retryable ends the request instead of spending the budget on it.**

Virtual models add a second path, because the router can select another eligible target when one fails, without interrupting the connected client. [Virtual models, routing, and failover](#virtual-models-routing-and-failover) describes target scoring and failover behavior.

#### Recovery after a restart

Workers claim durable queue items on leases that last 30 seconds ([`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_LEASE_TTL_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_LEASE_TTL_SEC)) and a sweep runs every 5 seconds ([`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_RECOVERY_SWEEP_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_RECOVERY_SWEEP_SEC)) to reclaim items whose lease expired, so work that was in flight when its worker died returns to the queue instead of staying claimed by a process that no longer exists.

At startup SoAI inspects the tasks still marked active and resolves each one. A task that still carries its orchestration context is requeued and runs again, a task that lost it is finalized as failed and reports that the server restarted while the task was in flight, and a task whose cancellation was already requested is finalized as cancelled with its recorded reason. The same pass repeats periodically while SoAI runs, which covers tasks orphaned by a worker failure rather than by a restart.

The WebUI handles a restart from the other side. It shows that SoAI is offline or restarting, asks you to keep the page open, and reconnects on its own with a delay that starts at 1 second and grows to at most 30. A script can check `/api/v1/system/health`, which reports `ok` or `degraded` and does not require authentication; the [HTTP API reference](#http-api-reference) documents it with the other management endpoints.

##### After an unclean shutdown

SoAI writes a marker file named `soai_process.dirty` in [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA) when the process starts and removes it only after a clean shutdown has finished. Finding that marker at the next start is how SoAI knows the previous run ended without one, which is the case after a crash, a host power loss, a forced host restart, or a process killed from a terminal. It then runs a [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) `PRAGMA quick_check` over the core database before the application starts serving, because the run that ended abruptly may have been in the middle of a write.

That check reads the whole database rather than sampling it, so on a large instance it can take several minutes, and the WebUI and the API are not available for any of them. Startup is not stuck: the lifecycle log records that the previous run did not shut down cleanly when the check begins, and records its successful completion before startup continues. Wait for it. Stopping SoAI or power-cycling the host while it runs leaves the marker in place, so the next start finds an unclean shutdown again and repeats the same check from the beginning, and each interruption also adds another unclean shutdown to recover from.

**If the check fails, SoAI stops instead of continuing, and it does not modify the damaged database on its own.** Treat that as a data-recovery situation rather than a startup problem, and follow [Recover a database that failed its integrity check](#recover-a-database-that-failed-its-integrity-check).

An unclean shutdown has a second consequence away from the database. When GPU settings were applied before the crash, the same start returns power, fan, and clock control to safe defaults and clears **Apply at boot** on every saved device, so a tuning profile that may have contributed to the crash is not reapplied on the way back up. [GPU controls and tuning](#gpu-controls-and-tuning) covers the saved slots and when to re-enable the boot profile.

#### Circuit breakers

Each plugin has a circuit breaker for inference dispatch, and it starts closed. SoAI counts qualifying failures inside the window set by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_WINDOW_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_WINDOW_SEC), 1,440 seconds by default, and drops failures older than that window from the count. Reaching [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_THRESHOLD`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_THRESHOLD), 3 by default, opens the circuit and blocks new dispatch to that plugin, while a success clears the accumulated count.

An open circuit holds until [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SEC) has passed since the last failure, 1,440 seconds by default, and then moves to half-open and admits one probe. A successful probe closes the circuit and clears its history, and a failed probe opens it again and restarts the cooldown.

SoAI writes changed breaker state to the database every 15 seconds. Startup resets persisted open and half-open circuits to closed, so a restarted backend evaluates plugin health again rather than inheriting an old verdict.

#### Plugin Guardian

The Guardian schedules health checks about every [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.INTERVAL_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.INTERVAL_SEC) seconds, 20 by default, with jitter spreading them across time. It pings idle plugins, watches long-running work, and detects plugins left in a transitional state. The default ping timeout is 15 seconds and the default transitional-state timeout is 900 seconds. It also detects repeated state changes through [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FLAPPING_WINDOW_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FLAPPING_WINDOW_SEC) and [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FLAPPING_MIN_TRANSITIONS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FLAPPING_MIN_TRANSITIONS).

Recovery attempts are counted consecutively rather than inside a time window. A successful health ping clears the counter, and so does resetting the circuit from Plugins. When the attempts exceed [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS), 3 by default, SoAI stops the backend where the runtime requires it, trips the circuit, and marks the plugin quarantined.

Each recovery attempt purges that plugin's queued and running tasks before it revalidates or restarts the backend, so requests already in flight on the affected plugin end with a failure you can see instead of waiting on a runtime that is being rebuilt. Work for other plugins is untouched.

#### What users see

In the SoAI WebUI, open **Dashboard** for overall health and current queue depth, and open **Plugins** to see a plugin's runtime status and circuit state. Select the plugin to open **Plugin information**, where the circuit state, failure count, last failure, and timeout are shown; a plugin with an open circuit also carries a banner saying the switch resets it. For the output behind a failed health check, open **Logs** from the **Settings** menu at the right of the header and select the Core or plugin source.

**An open circuit and a quarantine are not interchangeable.** An open circuit is a dispatch decision based on recent failures, while a quarantine is a runtime state the plugin reaches after recovery escalation or an integrity failure. Package compatibility, backend state, worker state, quarantine, and circuit state stay separate so the WebUI reports the actual failure instead of collapsing it into one generic status.

Correct the reported cause before you clear either state, since resetting a circuit while its failure remains only sends work back into it. [Reset an open circuit](#recover-an-unavailable-plugin) gives the WebUI procedure, including the distinct paths for an open circuit, an ordinary quarantine, and clone integrity recovery, and [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) maps a queue-full 503 and other symptoms to their causes.

### Operational runbooks [page: operational-runbooks]

These runbooks cover routine administration and recovery through the SoAI WebUI wherever it provides the required control, while the [HTTP API reference](#http-api-reference) covers the same management surfaces for scripts.

#### Starting and stopping SoAI

If SoAI is stopped, start it with the launcher for its installation. Once it is running, use the WebUI for routine power actions. Open Power and select **Restart application** to reload SoAI, or **Shut down application** to stop it while leaving the host running. **Read the confirmation before continuing because either action disconnects current WebUI sessions.**

After a restart, reconnect to the WebUI and confirm that the Dashboard reports a ready application state. After a shutdown, start SoAI with the same launcher used for the installation.

Shutdown first stops new work and drains API servers for the budget set by [`SYSTEM.SHUTDOWN.SERVER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-SYSTEM.SHUTDOWN.SERVER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_SEC). It then stops background services, plugins, the orchestrator, MCP services, terminal sessions, storage, metrics, and hardware services in their configured order. SoAI resolves accepted work and task finalizers before it closes shared HTTP and database resources.

Scripts can use the power control endpoints in the System API. Restart follows the same teardown sequence and then relaunches the application.

#### Recover a database that failed its integrity check

After an unclean shutdown SoAI runs a [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) `PRAGMA quick_check` over the core database before it starts serving, and a failed check ends startup at that point. The WebUI never becomes available, so the backup and restore controls inside it are out of reach and this recovery happens in a terminal against the files on disk. SoAI does not repair or rewrite the damaged database on its own, so it stays exactly as the failed run left it until you act on it. [After an unclean shutdown](#after-an-unclean-shutdown) describes when the check runs.

The commands below use the default [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) installation folder `/opt/soai`, where the database is `data/database/soai.db`, resolved from [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA) and [`DATA.DATABASE.PATHS.SYSTEM_DB`](#config-DATA.DATABASE.PATHS.SYSTEM_DB). [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) installs to `/Applications/SoAI` and [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) to the folder chosen during setup, and the layout inside is the same on all three. A service installation runs as root and its database files are readable only by their owner, so run every command as that account or through `sudo`.

You also need the [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) command-line shell, which a SoAI installation does not include. [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) and [Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/) install it with `sudo apt install sqlite3`, [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) already ships it, and [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) needs the precompiled command-line tools from the download page at [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/). Run `sqlite3 --version` and confirm 3.29 or later, because the `.recover` command this runbook depends on does not exist in earlier releases.

##### Stop SoAI and copy the database

Stop the service before anything else, and treat this as urgent on a service installation. SoAI exits in an orderly way after the failed check, and an orderly exit clears the unclean-shutdown marker that made it check at all, so the restart 10 seconds later finds nothing to verify and opens the damaged database as though the previous run had ended normally. An installation you start yourself needs its launcher instead, named for the edition and platform in the [Launcher and CLI reference](#launcher-and-cli-reference).

```bash
sudo systemctl stop soai.service

# An installation without the service
cd /opt/soai
./soai.sh --stop
./soai.sh --status

# SoAI OS
./soai_os/soai-os.sh --stop
./soai_os/soai-os.sh --status
```

Now take two copies of the database and its write-ahead log companions, onto a filesystem with room for both. The copy under `original` is the one version of your data that nothing later in this runbook touches, so leave it closed even to read it. Everything else happens under `work`.

```bash
mkdir -p /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/original /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/work
cd /opt/soai/data/database
cp -p soai.db soai.db-wal soai.db-shm /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/original/
cp -p soai.db soai.db-wal soai.db-shm /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/work/
```

The `-wal` and `-shm` files exist only while a write session was open, so `cp` reporting one of them as missing is normal and the copy is still complete. Keeping the whole set together matters because the `-wal` file holds committed transactions that are not in the database file yet.

##### Confirm the failure on the copy

Run the check SoAI ran, followed by the slower full check, against the working copy rather than the instance. Opening a database that still has a `-wal` file makes [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) replay that log into it, which is a write, so both the instance and the `original` copy stay closed.

```bash
cd /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/work
sqlite3 soai.db "PRAGMA quick_check;"
sqlite3 soai.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
```

A healthy database answers `ok` to both, and anything else is the damage that stopped startup. The critical message SoAI wrote before it exited is in the main log, named by [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH) and [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG).

**Do not restart SoAI to see whether the check passes on another attempt.** The check runs only when a start finds the `soai_process.dirty` marker that an unclean shutdown leaves behind, and the exit after a failed check removes that marker on its way out, so a second start does not repeat the check. It opens the damaged database instead and writes into it, which is the one thing that can still make this worse. Whatever you put back has to be verified here, in a terminal, because SoAI is not going to verify it for you.

##### Restore the database from a backup

A verified backup is the only path that returns a database whose contents are known to be good. Backups live under [`DATA.BACKUP.BACKUPS_PATH`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.BACKUPS_PATH) as one directory per backup named `soai_backup_<date>_<time>`, each holding its database at `data/database/soai.db` beside a `manifest.json` recording every captured file with its size and SHA-256. SoAI writes the backup as a consistent database copy rather than a raw file copy, so it arrives without a `-wal` companion to carry over.

Each manifest also records the integrity result SoAI observed while writing that backup, which narrows the candidates without reading a single database. Verify the one you choose anyway, since the manifest describes the file as it was written rather than as it is now. That verification reads the whole database, so on a large instance give it time.

```bash
cd /opt/soai/data/backups
grep -l '"sqlite_integrity_ok": true' soai_backup_*/manifest.json
sqlite3 soai_backup_20260903_142824/data/database/soai.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
```

Work backwards from the newest backup until one answers `ok`, then put that file in place. The damaged files are already preserved in `/var/tmp/soai-db-rescue`, so removing them from the instance costs nothing. The `-wal` and `-shm` files belong to the database you are removing, and [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) can replay a leftover log into whatever database takes its place, so they go with it.

```bash
cd /opt/soai
rm -f data/database/soai.db data/database/soai.db-wal data/database/soai.db-shm
cp -p data/backups/soai_backup_20260903_142824/data/database/soai.db data/database/soai.db
```

Do not substitute a symbolic link for the database file, because SoAI rejects one. It also restores the restrictive file mode on the database, its companions, and their directory each time it opens them, so the copy needs no permission fixing afterwards.

This returns the database alone. Configuration, plugin configuration, GPU settings, the encryption key that protects secrets stored in the database, and user files are all still whatever the failed instance left behind, and they can be newer than the database you just installed. Once SoAI is running again, use [Restore](#restore) on the same backup to bring all of it back to one consistent point.

##### Salvage the database when no backup is usable

The [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) `.recover` command reads whatever pages it can still parse and writes them out as SQL statements, which you load into a new file. Run it against the working copy and never in place over a database you want to keep, allow room for a second full-size database, and expect a large instance to take a while. The target file has to be absent or empty, so the `rm` below clears anything an earlier attempt left behind.

```bash
cd /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/work
rm -f soai-recovered.db
sqlite3 soai.db ".recover" | sqlite3 soai-recovered.db
sqlite3 soai-recovered.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
sqlite3 soai-recovered.db "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'lost_and_found';"
```

On [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/), redirect through a file instead of piping between the two commands.

```bat
del recovered.sql soai-recovered.db
sqlite3.exe soai.db ".recover" > recovered.sql
sqlite3.exe soai-recovered.db < recovered.sql
sqlite3.exe soai-recovered.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
```

The recovered file passing `integrity_check` means only that it is now a well-formed database, not that it still holds your data. Rows on a page [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) could not read are gone, and rows it could read but could not return to their own table land in a `lost_and_found` table, which is what the third command looks for. If `.recover` produces nothing usable, `.dump` is worth one attempt, although it stops at the first page it cannot read rather than working around it. This step can cost data permanently, so decide what the recovered file is worth before you install it.

```bash
cd /opt/soai
rm -f data/database/soai.db data/database/soai.db-wal data/database/soai.db-shm
cp -p /var/tmp/soai-db-rescue/work/soai-recovered.db data/database/soai.db
```

##### Return the instance to service

Start SoAI with the launcher for the installation, or start the service again. The launcher starts SoAI when you give it no command at all.

```bash
cd /opt/soai
./soai.sh

# SoAI OS
./soai_os/soai-os.sh

# Service installations
sudo systemctl start soai.service
```

This start finds no unclean-shutdown marker and so runs no integrity check of its own, which is why the file you installed had to answer `ok` before it went into place. Sign in, confirm that the Dashboard reports a ready application state, and confirm that the users, conversations, models, and plugin configuration you expect are all there. A restored backup should be complete as of the moment it was taken. A recovered database is the one to read carefully, because that is where `.recover` may have dropped rows.

Corruption reported here is usually a symptom of the host rather than of the database. Before the instance goes back into normal use, check for an unstable overclock or undervolt, failing memory, and storage device or filesystem errors, because a host that damaged the database once will do it again. [Backup](#backup) covers the policy that decides how much work a future failure can cost.

#### Working with plugins

Open Plugins to manage a plugin and its backend. Use the plugin switch to enable or disable it. Use **Stop plugin** when you need to halt its running backend without uninstalling anything. For a local engine, use **Install backend** or **Manage backend**. Use **Edit configuration** for plugin-specific settings and GPU binding.

Disable a plugin when you need the scheduler to keep it offline during maintenance. Use **Stop plugin** to end its current backend process. **A stopped plugin remains enabled, so SoAI may start it again for later work.** Follow the task in the Tasks panel and wait for a terminal result before continuing. The plugin stop command has a 300-second default budget, set by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.COMMAND_TIMEOUTS_SEC.PLUGIN_STOP`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.COMMAND_TIMEOUTS_SEC.PLUGIN_STOP).

##### Reset an open circuit

An open circuit blocks new dispatch after repeated qualifying failures. Reset it from Plugins after you correct the cause.

1. Open Plugins and select the affected plugin to open **Plugin information**.
2. Read the status and circuit-breaker details. Then correct the reported backend, provider, configuration, storage, or package problem.
3. Return to the plugin card. Its circuit-breaker banner states that the switch will reset the circuit. Turn on the switch and wait for the reset task to finish.
4. Confirm that the banner is gone. If the plugin owns a model, open that model from Models, select **Test model**, and confirm that the test succeeds.

Do not reset a circuit before fixing the underlying failure. The default threshold is three consecutive failures, controlled by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_THRESHOLD`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAILURE_THRESHOLD).

##### Make a quarantined plugin available again

A quarantined plugin with no circuit-breaker banner has a locked switch and no reset control on its card. Restarting SoAI clears an ordinary recovery quarantine and runs the startup checks again. A clone integrity quarantine remains in place until the failed clone is recovered or removed.

1. Open Plugins and select the quarantined plugin to open **Plugin information**.
2. Confirm its status, then open **Logs** from the **Settings** menu at the right of the header and select that plugin's source. Check **Tasks** for a failed clone operation.
3. Correct the backend, provider, configuration, storage, package, or clone problem shown there.
4. Open Power and select **Restart application**. Read the confirmation and select **Restart application** again.
5. Wait for the WebUI to reconnect, then return to Plugins.
6. Confirm that the plugin no longer shows **Quarantined**. If its switch is off, turn it on. If the backend needs attention, use **Install backend** or **Manage backend** on its card.
7. If the plugin owns a model, open that model from Models, select **Test model**, and confirm that the test succeeds.

If the plugin still shows **Quarantined** after restart and Tasks contains a failed clone operation, treat it as clone integrity recovery. A circuit reset does not clear that state, and startup preserves it while the clone remains inconsistent. The WebUI has no force-clear action. Keep the clone if you need its files for diagnosis or recovery.

If you do not need the damaged clone, open Plugins, select **Delete plugin** on that clone, review the deletion warning, and select **Delete**. Then open the source plugin, select **Clone plugin**, choose whether to copy its models, and select **Clone**. Verify that the replacement appears on Plugins without a quarantine status.

#### Model downloads, discovery, and deletion

Open Models and select **Add model** to download a model. Choose the plugin, enter the model download ID, select a variant when the plugin offers one, and select **Download model**. Follow progress in the Tasks panel. [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE) blocks downloads when enabled.

To refresh the catalog after you place model files in the models folder, open Models, select **Add model**, switch to **Add model manually**, and select **Discover models**. SoAI also runs discovery after backend installation, model downloads, and plugin enable operations.

To remove a model, open it from Models, select **Delete model**, and read the warning. Confirm when you intend to remove the listed data. The owning plugin decides which local files or provider records the operation removes.

#### Watching logs and cancelling tasks

Open **Logs** from the **Settings** menu at the right of the header to inspect current Core and plugin output. Select the Core or plugin source, choose how many lines to display, and keep the view open while reproducing a failure. Use the Tasks panel in the WebUI header to inspect running operations.

To cancel an operation, open Tasks and select **Cancel running task** when that control is available for the entry. Cancellation is a request, so wait for the final status before retrying. **Stop all activity** appears only when the panel contains a stoppable non-persistent plugin or visible cancelable operation; persistent plugins cannot be stopped from this panel. See [Tasks and notifications](#tasks-and-notifications) for the panel controls and outcomes.

#### Authenticating a management script

Most System API routes at `/api/v1/*` require authentication. Explicit public routes include system health, information, limits, and license data; the setup-status endpoint; login; MCP OAuth metadata and callback routes; and the [Telegram](https://telegram.org/) and [WhatsApp](https://www.whatsapp.com/) messaging webhooks. The System API schema lists the available routes.

The WebUI creates `soai-http-token` and `soai-http-csrf` cookies over HTTP. Over HTTPS, it uses `__Host-soai-token` and `__Host-soai-csrf`. A script that signs in through the WebUI login flow must retain both cookies. For cookie-authenticated `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE` requests to protected routes, copy the CSRF cookie value into the `X-SoAI-CSRF` header.

API keys created by selecting the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then **Settings > [OpenAI](https://openai.com/)**, apply to OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible routes under `/v1/*`, not the System API. After setup, those compatible routes are open while no API keys exist. **Creating the first key makes a key mandatory for every `/v1/*` call.** Send it as a `Bearer` token to OpenAI-compatible endpoints; Anthropic-compatible endpoints also accept `x-api-key`.

### System power and application lifecycle [page: system-power-and-application-lifecycle]

**Power** in the SoAI WebUI separates application lifecycle actions from actions that affect the entire host. It is available only to an Administrator with **System power control** ([`SYSTEM_POWER`](#acl-SYSTEM_POWER)). On a fresh installation it is shown in the sidebar for an eligible Administrator.

#### Choose the correct scope

| Action | Effect | Options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Restart application** | Restarts SoAI and its services. The host stays running. | Delay in seconds, default 0 |
| **Shut down application** | Stops SoAI. Another host process or service must start it again. | Delay in seconds, default 10 |
| **Restart system** | Reboots the whole host and reloads the operating system. | Delay in seconds, default 10; optional **Force restart** |
| **Shut down system** | Stops host processes and powers off the machine. | Delay in seconds, default 10; optional **Force shutdown** |
| **Suspend system** | Pauses processes in a low-power state until the host resumes. | Delay in seconds, default 10 |
| **Hibernate system** | Saves memory to disk and powers off most hardware. | Delay in seconds, default 10 |

#### Run an action

1. Open **Power** and set the delay or force option on the intended card.
2. Select the action button and read the confirmation. System actions warn that they affect the whole machine.
3. Confirm. An accepted delayed shutdown, suspend, or hibernate can show a countdown with **Cancel**.
4. Keep the page open if you need to observe the accepted operation. The status progresses through scheduled, executing, and a truthful terminal state.

A restart-required notice can replace the delay control on the relevant restart card and state the first recorded reason. Use application restart for ordinary SoAI configuration changes. A SoAI OS operation can explicitly require a full system restart.

#### Host actions are conditional

**The page lists the host action cards, but acceptance still depends on runtime policy and operating-system support.** When [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED) is enabled, SoAI rejects restart, shutdown, suspend, and hibernate requests for the host. A platform that cannot construct the requested system command also rejects that action. The WebUI reports the failure; it does not pretend the host changed state.

**Force restart** and **Force shutdown** can interrupt other host work. Use them only when a normal operation cannot complete and you have accounted for active tasks, database writes, model downloads, and other users.

A forced action also has a cost on the way back up, because SoAI treats the run it ended as an unclean shutdown. The next start verifies the core database before it serves anything, which can take several minutes on a large instance, and it returns saved GPU settings to safe defaults. [After an unclean shutdown](#after-an-unclean-shutdown) describes what to expect and why the check should not be interrupted.

### Backup [page: backup]

In the SoAI WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and open **Backup** to create a recovery point before an upgrade, a storage move, or another change that affects the instance. The **Backup** tab is available only to an Administrator with **Backup administration** ([`BACKUP_ADMIN`](#acl-BACKUP_ADMIN)). It is not shown to Standard users.

#### Create and verify a backup

1. Select **Create backup**, then confirm the request.
2. Wait for the progress indicator to finish. While a backup task is running, the backup actions are unavailable.
3. In **Available backups**, find the new entry. It shows its ID, creation time, size, and a **Valid** or **Invalid** status.
4. Select **Verify** before relying on a backup for recovery or before taking a copy off the host.

**Verify** and **Restore** are available only for a backup marked **Valid**. An **Invalid** entry is not a recovery point. Resolve the reported backup issue and create a new backup instead of attempting a restore from it.

#### Download a copy

Select **Download** beside a completed backup to save an archive named after its backup ID with a `.tar.gz` extension. Keep that archive somewhere other than the SoAI host if it is part of your disaster-recovery plan. **The WebUI lists the backups in SoAI's managed backup store; it does not offer an archive import control.**

#### What a managed backup includes

The default target set includes the primary database, active Core configuration, the system encryption key, plugin sidecar configuration, user data, and saved GPU settings slots. User data includes the managed files and wallpaper directories when they exist. Application and plugin logs are excluded by default.

**A downloaded backup is a sensitive, unencrypted `.tar.gz` archive.** Because the default targets include both application data and the installation encryption key, anyone who obtains the archive may be able to read stored data and decrypt persisted secrets. Keep downloaded copies on access-controlled storage, do not place them in a shared folder or source repository, and read [Protect backups and the installation key](#backup-security).

An Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) can review the target set by selecting the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then selecting **Settings** from its menu. Select **Advanced** in the page header, select the **Data** tab, then open the **Backup** group. The **Targets** group contains the individual switches. See [`DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.DATABASE`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.DATABASE) through [`DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.LOGS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.TARGETS.LOGS) for the full list and defaults.

#### Set the automatic policy

The same **Data > Backup** area controls whether managed backups are enabled, the schedule, and retention. The factory policy is enabled, attempts a backup every 24 hours, keeps up to seven completed backups, and removes completed backups older than 720 hours. You can change **Interval hours**, **Run on startup**, **On shutdown**, **Max backups**, and **Max age hours**, then select **Save**.

Review the exact behavior and defaults in [`DATA.BACKUP.ENABLED`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.ENABLED), [`DATA.BACKUP.SCHEDULE.INTERVAL_HOURS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.SCHEDULE.INTERVAL_HOURS), [`DATA.BACKUP.RETENTION.MAX_BACKUPS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.RETENTION.MAX_BACKUPS), and [`DATA.BACKUP.RETENTION.MAX_AGE_HOURS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.RETENTION.MAX_AGE_HOURS).

### Restore [page: restore]

Restoring a selected valid backup replaces the current copies of the data it contains, then restarts SoAI. Use it to recover a known-good instance state, not as a way to inspect a backup. **The action overwrites current data and cannot be undone in the WebUI.**

#### Prepare for a restore

1. In the SoAI WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and select **Backup**. This tab is available only to an Administrator with **Backup administration** ( [`BACKUP_ADMIN`](#acl-BACKUP_ADMIN) ).
2. Create a new backup of the current state if you may need to return to it.
3. Select **Verify** for the backup you intend to restore.
4. Confirm that the entry shows **Valid**, then make sure users can tolerate an interruption while SoAI restarts.

The backup list shows each backup's ID, creation time, size, and validity. The **Restore** button is disabled for entries marked **Invalid**.

#### Restore the backup

1. In **Available backups**, select **Restore** beside the valid backup.
2. Read the confirmation. It explicitly warns that current data will be overwritten.
3. Select **Restore** to start the task and leave the page open until its progress finishes.
4. When the restore succeeds, SoAI starts its restart flow. Wait for the WebUI to become available again, then sign in and check the settings, plugin configuration, and user data you need.

SoAI disables the other backup actions while a backup operation is running. **Do not start another backup, restore, verification, download, or deletion task until the current task reaches a result.**

#### If a restore does not finish

The Backup tab reports a failed restore task instead of presenting it as complete. Do not retry immediately against the same backup. Check the task result and confirm that the backup is still **Valid**. If you have **Log access** ([`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS)), open **Logs** from the **Settings** menu at the right of the header. Logs can also appear in the sidebar if it has been added there. Use the operational runbooks to investigate disk space, permissions, or host failures. If the backup is no longer valid, create or use a different verified recovery point.

#### What is restored

SoAI restores the files recorded in the selected backup's manifest. **The target switches that are enabled now affect new backups; changing them does not add or remove content from an existing backup.** Restore writes each recorded item to the current configured destination for that data type.

With factory target settings, a newly created backup contains the primary database, Core configuration, encryption key, plugin configuration, user data, and saved GPU settings slots. Logs are excluded by default. Review the target settings before creating a recovery point that must contain a particular data set.

### Updating SoAI [page: updating-soai]

Update a running installation from the SoAI WebUI. With **Software updates** ([`SOFTWARE_UPDATE`](#acl-SOFTWARE_UPDATE)), open the **Settings** menu at the right of the header and select **Updates**. If the Dashboard's **Quick actions** section is visible, its **Updates** shortcut opens the same page. Application updates are separate from plugin-backend updates and, on SoAI OS, from host package updates.

#### Prepare and install an update

The **Backup** tab appears only to an Administrator with **Backup administration** ([`BACKUP_ADMIN`](#acl-BACKUP_ADMIN)).

1. Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and select **Backup**.
2. Select **Create backup**.
3. Keep a downloaded copy outside the host when your recovery policy requires one.

**An update transaction protects the application files it changes, but it is not a substitute for a backup of data and configuration.**

##### Install an application update

1. On **Updates**, select **Check for updates**.
2. In **SoAI application updates**, review the current version, latest version, release notes, and release link.
3. On a supported [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/), [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/), or [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) installation, select **Install update** and confirm the dialog.
4. Wait for the updating screen to reconnect before using SoAI again.

The update service checks the signed release manifest, its signing key, the selected edition, and the downloaded release artifact before applying it. It stages the change in an update transaction and keeps rollback data until the updated application completes startup successfully. SoAI restarts the application when the update was started from a running instance.

##### Conditions that disable automatic updates

**The WebUI cannot check or install an application update when [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE) is enabled.** Automatic application updates are also unavailable when [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED) disables host actions. Core automatic installation supports [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) x64 and ARM64, [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) and [Apple](https://www.apple.com/) silicon, and [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) x64. [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) and [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) use complete archives. [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) verifies and hands off the release installer, which preserves the existing data directory and replaces the launcher and application files in place.

#### Edition boundaries and recovery

An application update stays within the installed edition. **It cannot switch Core into the appliance edition or the reverse.** In an appliance installation, the **SoAI OS updates** section handles host package updates separately; continue with [the appliance update guide](#soai-os-package-updates) for that workflow.

##### Recover from an unsuccessful update

**Do not begin another update while the previous transaction may still be recovering.** If the WebUI does not reconnect, use the matching launcher to check status, preserve the reported error, and follow the [Operational runbooks](#operational-runbooks). Restore a verified backup only when recovery of the installation cannot retain the required data.

Use [Reset and account recovery](#reset-and-account-recovery) only when the failure is caused by a specific damaged setting or when you deliberately intend to clear managed data; an update failure does not by itself justify a factory reset.

### Reset and account recovery [page: reset-and-account-recovery]

The Reset tab clears a selected category of data. It is for recovery and deliberate cleanup, not routine maintenance. In the SoAI WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and select **Reset**. Read the action description before choosing its **Reset** button. Each action asks for confirmation, and **Factory reset** ([`FACTORY_RESET`](#acl-FACTORY_RESET)) asks twice. For a failed application update, begin with [the update recovery guidance](#updating-soai) before clearing any data.

#### Who can use the Reset tab

**Settings > Reset** is shown only to an Administrator. The page hides **Metrics** and **Hardware** without **Metrics reset** ([`METRICS_RESET`](#acl-METRICS_RESET)), **Configuration** without **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)), and **Factory reset** ([`FACTORY_RESET`](#acl-FACTORY_RESET)) without that permission. Resetting **ACL policy** also requires **ACL administration** ([`ACL_ADMIN`](#acl-ACL_ADMIN)). Resetting **Appearance** requires **UI customization** ([`WEBUI_APPEARANCE_ADMIN`](#acl-WEBUI_APPEARANCE_ADMIN)) because it removes the shared wallpaper.

#### Choose the smallest reset that solves the problem

| Reset action | Result |
| --- | --- |
| **ACL policy** | Restores access-control policy overrides to their defaults. |
| **Appearance** | Removes the shared wallpaper and restores the current user's color, glass, animation, and appearance-effect settings. |
| **Metrics** | Resets in-memory metrics and live persistence. Historical time-series data remains available. |
| **Hardware** | Removes recorded hardware-monitoring and SoAIBench history. |
| **Page layouts** | Restores saved Dashboard, Metrics, and Hardware movable layouts. |
| **WebUI** | Restores the signed-in user's non-advanced WebUI preferences, including appearance, language, layout, and related preferences. |
| **Chat presets** | Deletes the signed-in user's saved chat configuration presets. Existing conversations and the open chat configuration remain unchanged. |
| **Prompt history** | Deletes the signed-in user's saved server-side chat prompt history. |
| **Recent searches** | Clears the recent searches shown on the Search page. |
| **Tool approvals** | Forgets the signed-in user's remembered approval decisions. SoAI asks again when a tool requires approval. |
| **[Password manager](#passwords-and-credential-tools)** | Deletes the signed-in user's saved password-vault credentials and invalidates active secure handles. |
| **Conversations** | Deletes the signed-in user's chat conversations and automation transcripts. Automations, settings, models, and plugins remain. |
| **Configuration** | Restores advanced and core configuration to built-in defaults, preserves non-configuration data, and restarts SoAI. |
| **Factory reset** ([`FACTORY_RESET`](#acl-FACTORY_RESET)) | Deletes managed user data, settings, models, backups, and non-built-in plugins, then restarts to the initial setup state. |

#### Reset configuration or return to factory state

**Configuration** is the right choice when configuration is the only problem. It removes the managed active configuration file and its recovery copies during restart, then SoAI recreates the active file from the built-in default. The action requires **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) and is blocked when [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HOST_SYSTEM_ACTIONS_DISABLED) is enabled.

Use **Factory reset** ([`FACTORY_RESET`](#acl-FACTORY_RESET)) only when you intend to remove managed application data. Before confirming it, create a backup from the **Backup** tab and keep any downloaded copy outside the SoAI installation. The action has the same host-action policy check and requires that permission. **It deletes only application-managed paths inside the installation; configured data paths outside the installation are not deleted.** After the second confirmation, the WebUI redirects to sign-in while SoAI restarts. When the WebUI detects the fresh installation state, it opens the setup wizard.

#### Change or recover a login password

The **Users** tab is available only to an Administrator with **User administration** ([`USER_ADMIN`](#acl-USER_ADMIN)). Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and select **Users**. Select **Password** for the account, enter **Your current password**, then enter and confirm the new password. A Standard account has no self-service **Users**-tab path. New passwords must contain at least 8 characters and no more than 1024 characters.

When no administrator can sign in, [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) and [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) installations can use the POSIX launcher recovery command. Stop SoAI first, run the command from the installation directory, then start it again. The command asks for the new password twice without echoing it.

```bash
# SoAI on Linux
./soai.sh --stop
./soai.sh --reset-user-password administrator
./soai.sh --start

# SoAI on macOS
sudo /Applications/SoAI/soai.command --stop
sudo /Applications/SoAI/soai.command --reset-user-password administrator
sudo /Applications/SoAI/soai.command --start

# SoAI OS
./soai_os/soai-os.sh --stop
./soai_os/soai-os.sh --reset-user-password administrator
./soai_os/soai-os.sh --start
```

**The [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) release launcher does not provide `--reset-user-password`.** Do not edit the database to work around a missing administrator account.

### Data storage, retention, and relocation [page: data-storage-retention-and-relocation]

SoAI keeps durable state under one system-data root by default. The database, managed files, model downloads, plugin runtimes, logs, backups, knowledge indexes, browser state, and WebUI media use separate paths beneath that root. **Changing a path does not move existing data.**

#### Understand storage paths

[`SYSTEM.PATHS.BASE`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.BASE) is the installation base used to resolve base-relative paths, with an empty value selecting the installation directory. [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA) defaults to `data` under that base, and most state paths are then resolved under the system-data directory. **Every path listed below requires a restart after it changes.**

##### Know what each durable path owns

| Stored data | Configuration path | Factory-relative location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary database | [`DATA.DATABASE.PATHS.SYSTEM_DB`](#config-DATA.DATABASE.PATHS.SYSTEM_DB) | `database/soai.db` |
| Encryption key for protected values | [`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_ENCRYPTION_KEY`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_ENCRYPTION_KEY) | `secret.key` |
| Managed user files | [`DATA.FILES.PATHS.FILES_STORAGE`](#config-DATA.FILES.PATHS.FILES_STORAGE) | `files` |
| Downloaded model files | [`MODELS.MANAGER.PATHS.MODELS`](#config-MODELS.MANAGER.PATHS.MODELS) | `models` |
| Managed plugin backends | [`PLUGINS.PATHS.BACKENDS`](#config-PLUGINS.PATHS.BACKENDS) | `backends` |
| Plugin environments | [`PLUGINS.PATHS.VENVS_ROOT`](#config-PLUGINS.PATHS.VENVS_ROOT) | `plugins/venvs` |
| Application logs | [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH) | `logs` |
| Managed backups | [`DATA.BACKUP.BACKUPS_PATH`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.BACKUPS_PATH) | `backups` |
| Knowledge vector index | [`TOOLS.RAG.CHROMA_PATH`](#config-TOOLS.RAG.CHROMA_PATH) | `chroma_rag` |
| Knowledge sparse index | [`TOOLS.RAG.SPARSE_INDEX_DIR`](#config-TOOLS.RAG.SPARSE_INDEX_DIR) | `rag_sparse_index` |
| Browser cookies and origin storage | [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.STORAGE_STATE_DIR`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.STORAGE_STATE_DIR) | `browser-storage-state` |
| Persistent browser profiles | [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.USER_DATA_DIR_BASE_DIR`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.USER_DATA_DIR_BASE_DIR) | `browser-user-data` |
| Shared wallpaper | [`SERVER.WEBUI.WALLPAPER_STORAGE_PATH`](#config-SERVER.WEBUI.WALLPAPER_STORAGE_PATH) | `wallpaper` |

Installed `.soaiplugin` packages are different. Their [`PLUGINS.PATHS.PLUGINS`](#config-PLUGINS.PATHS.PLUGINS) path is resolved under the installation base, not under system data.

#### Plan and relocate data

Model files and plugin runtimes usually dominate storage use. Managed files, knowledge indexes, browser profiles, logs, metrics history, and backups grow with use. A backup can temporarily require substantial free space in both its source and destination. **Keep the database and encryption key together in the recovery plan; protected values cannot be recovered from the database alone.**

SoAI reserves disk space before supported large writes and rejects work that would violate its reserve. See [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) for reserve settings and workload sizing.

##### Relocate data safely

Editing Advanced Settings requires **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)). Choose a maintenance window: the safe sequence saves the new path, stops SoAI before the restart, copies the data, and then starts SoAI with the saved path. Do not use SoAI between saving the path and stopping the service.

1. Create and verify a SoAI backup. Export a copy off the host.
2. In the SoAI WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then **Settings**. Select **Advanced** in the page header.
3. Paste the complete configuration path from the table above into the settings search. Confirm that the result is the path you intend to move.
4. Enter the destination and select **Save**. Use an absolute path when ownership or mount boundaries would otherwise be unclear.
5. When **Restart SoAI** appears, do not select it yet. Stop SoAI immediately with the launcher for the installed edition.
6. Copy the complete source to the saved destination, preserving permissions. Keep the original copy.
7. Start SoAI with the same edition launcher. The saved path takes effect during startup.
8. Wait for readiness, sign in, and verify the affected models, files, knowledge collections, browser state, plugin state, or logs.
9. Remove the old copy only after the new location and a restore test are known to work.

**Do not change a path while the service is writing to it, and do not assume a configuration edit migrates existing content.** For a complete move between installations, prefer the supported backup and restore workflow over manual selection of database-related files.
