### Getting help and reporting an issue [page: getting-help-and-reporting-an-issue]

Start on the page where the failure appeared, then collect only the diagnostic material needed to reproduce it. A useful report identifies the SoAI version, platform, affected operation, final status, and relevant Core or plugin log lines without including secrets. The **System information** report on Hardware is the fastest way to package environment details, but it does not replace reproduction steps or focused logs.

#### Use diagnostics in the SoAI WebUI

1. In the SoAI WebUI, open **Dashboard** to check overall service, plugin, model, queue, storage, and hardware state.
2. Open the affected feature and read its operation status or recorded reason.
3. Select the bell at the right of the header, then select **Tasks** to inspect work that is still running or awaiting cancellation.
4. Open **Logs** from the **Settings** button at the right of the header, choose Core or the affected plugin, and reproduce the failure once.
5. Open **Hardware** and select **Info** in the page header to generate a **System information** report.
6. Open **About** from the **Settings** button when you need only the displayed SoAI version and platform.

Dashboard requires **System status access** ([`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ)), and individual cards can require additional resource access. Hardware requires **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)), while its System information report also requests system status, system health, and installed plugin data, so the report requires [`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ), [`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ), and [`PLUGIN_READ`](#acl-PLUGIN_READ). Logs requires **Log access** ([`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS)). About requires [`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ) and [`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ).

The default sidebar layout hides **Settings**, **Logs**, and **About**. Open them from the **Settings** button at the right of the header. To add eligible pages to the sidebar, open **Settings**, select **Theme**, then find **Sidebar**. At **Visible pages**, select **Edit**, enable the pages you want, then select **Save**. **Changing sidebar visibility does not grant access to a page.**

#### Create a system information report

1. Open **Hardware** from the side navigation and select **Info** in the page header.
2. Wait for **System information** to finish generating, then review the displayed plain-text report.
3. Enable **Anonymize** if the report will leave your trusted environment.
4. Select **Copy** to place the displayed version on the clipboard, or select **Download** to save it as a `soai-system-info-<timestamp>.txt` file.

The report is designed to be pasted into a [GitHub](https://github.com/) issue or attached to another support report. It combines the current hardware, system information, system health, and installed plugin snapshots, including the operating system and architecture, uptime, memory and swap, CPU and GPU names and readings, network interfaces, disk mounts and usage, hardware capabilities, plugin versions and states, and SoAI health information. **It does not open or submit an issue, upload the report, collect logs, or add reproduction steps for you.**

**Anonymize** is off each time the modal opens. When enabled, it replaces common hostnames, email addresses, network addresses, URL credentials and sensitive query values, device and serial identifiers, UUIDs, user paths, mount paths, and parts of timestamps and uptime values. The displayed text changes immediately, and **Copy** or **Download** uses that anonymized version. It preserves most diagnostic specifications so the report remains useful, and it deliberately leaves SoAI installation paths unchanged. Unrecognized identifiers, proprietary plugin or device names, and other private strings can remain, so inspect the final displayed report and remove anything sensitive before sharing it. The toggle applies only to the System information report, not to logs, configuration excerpts, screenshots, or other attachments.

#### Build a reproducible report

- Describe what you selected or sent, what you expected, and what happened.
- Include the exact final status, HTTP status, task ID, trace ID, or reference ID shown by SoAI.
- State whether the problem affects Core, one plugin, one model, one browser, or every client.
- Attach the reviewed System information report. Add the relevant GPU driver and any model or provider details that the generated report does not contain.
- Attach only the log window and configuration fields needed to reproduce the failure.

Remove API keys, passwords, cookies, authorization headers, provider credentials, private prompts, personal data, proprietary file contents, and unrelated configuration values from every attachment. Replace each removed value with a label so the report remains understandable. **Do not send a full configuration export unless an approved private support channel explicitly requires it.**

#### Choose the right destination

| Problem | Destination |
| --- | --- |
| Known symptom or operational failure | [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) and [Operational runbooks](#operational-runbooks) |
| Reproducible product bug | Open the [SoAI repository](https://github.com/GetSoAI/SoAI), then select **Issues**. |
| Undisclosed vulnerability | [Security updates and vulnerability reporting](#security-updates-and-vulnerability-reporting) |
| License state or activation | [Licensing administration](#licensing-administration) |

**Do not place an undisclosed vulnerability or live credential in a public issue.** The public issue tracker is for non-sensitive product defects that other contributors can safely inspect.

## Hardware

### Hardware compatibility [page: hardware-compatibility]

Hardware compatibility depends on the SoAI edition and platform, then on the selected plugin, model, driver, and resources available on the host. Use the Hardware page to see what the current installation reports before choosing a model or changing a GPU setting.

#### Supported platform paths

| Edition and platform | Current installation path |
| --- | --- |
| SoAI Core on [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) | The published [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) archive supports 64-bit x64 and ARM64 hosts running [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) 12 or 13 or [Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/) 24.x or 26.x. |
| SoAI Core on [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) | The published complete archive supports [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) and [Apple](https://www.apple.com/) silicon and provides an in-application update path. |
| SoAI Core on [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) | The published installer supports 64-bit [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) 10 or later on x64. There is no [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) ARM64 installer. |
| SoAI OS | The appliance edition uses a UEFI [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) 13 [KDE](https://kde.org/) image for AMD64 and ARM64 hosts. |

**Platform support does not guarantee a particular inference backend or GPU feature.** Check the backend's own requirements and the model's memory needs before deploying it.

#### System requirements

SoAI works on CPU-only machines and on machines with one or more GPUs. A GPU is optional, but it is needed for reasonable local inference speeds.

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU | [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) Core i5-2500 or [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) FX-6100 | [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) Core i7-6700 or [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) Ryzen 5 1600 |
| RAM | 4 GB DDR3 | 16 GB DDR4 |
| Storage | 128 GB SATA SSD (SoAI occupies about 5 GB when freshly installed) | 512 GB NVMe SSD (SoAI occupies about 5 GB when freshly installed) |
| GPU | Optional compatible [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) Pascal-generation GeForce GTX 10-series, Quadro P-series, or Tesla P-series cards; or an [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) or [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) GPU supported by the selected backend's [ROCm](https://www.amd.com/), [Vulkan](https://www.vulkan.org/), XPU, [SYCL](https://www.khronos.org/sycl/), [OpenVINO](https://www.intel.com/), or [OpenCL](https://www.khronos.org/opencl/) runtime | Compatible [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) Ampere-generation GeForce RTX 30-series, RTX A-series, or Ampere data-center cards; [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) Radeon RX 6000/7000-series or Instinct MI200/MI300-series GPUs; or [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) Arc A-series/B-series or Data Center GPU Max cards |
| Operating system | [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) 12 or 13, [Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/) 24.x or 26.x, [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) 10 or 11, [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) Server 2016, 2019, 2022, or 2025, or [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) | [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) 13, [Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/) 26.x, [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) 11, [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) Server 2025, or [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) |

RAM and VRAM needs depend on the selected model, quantization, context length, plugin, and concurrency rather than on SoAI alone. Larger models and concurrent requests need more memory. Model files, plugin backends, databases, user files, backups, and working space also need storage beyond the application itself.

SoAI can run from a hard disk drive (HDD), SD card, or USB drive, but those storage types are not recommended and do not meet the SSD-based minimum or recommended storage tiers. Their lower throughput, higher latency, and removable-media failure risks can affect model loading, database activity, indexing, updates, backups, and concurrent file operations. Use an SSD for a normal installation and durable data paths.

Use an enterprise SSD for heavy or enterprise workloads. For maximum persistent-storage performance, an [Intel Optane](https://www.intel.com/) drive is the best option where available. A RAM drive can be used for maximum performance, but it is not recommended.

##### Use NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs together

SoAI supports mixed-vendor hosts containing [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/), [AMD](https://www.amd.com/), and [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) GPUs. Hardware inventory keeps a global device identity and a vendor-local binding index for every detected card, so monitoring and capability discovery do not assume that all GPUs come from one vendor. Full telemetry and controls still require the matching vendor driver and management tool.

[CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone) binding accepts only [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) GPUs, [ROCm](https://www.amd.com/) binding accepts only [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) GPUs, and XPU binding accepts only [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) GPUs. To use those vendors concurrently, run separate compatible plugin instances or backends and bind each one to GPUs from its runtime family. A [Vulkan](https://www.vulkan.org/) backend follows the devices exposed by its [Vulkan](https://www.vulkan.org/) runtime. Mixed-vendor support does not make one [CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone), [ROCm](https://www.amd.com/), or XPU backend span incompatible vendors.

#### Check a host in the SoAI WebUI

1. Open **Hardware** from the side navigation.
2. Review the live CPU, memory, storage, network, and GPU data that the host reports.
3. Use **Chart** to select a device and metric when you need a time-based view.
4. If the **GPU control** panel appears, inspect its per-device controls and ranges rather than assuming that another GPU supports the same settings.

Opening the page requires **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)). An Administrator with **ACL administration** ([`ACL_ADMIN`](#acl-ACL_ADMIN)) can grant that permission to a Standard user. Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu and select **ACL**. Open **Standard user**, enable **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)), and select **Save**. The GPU control panel also requires **GPU tuning** ([`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING)), which is an Administrator permission. The process panel requires **Process viewing** ([`HW_PROCESS_VIEW`](#acl-HW_PROCESS_VIEW)).

#### Why a metric or control can be absent

SoAI can identify a GPU before complete telemetry is available. Missing vendor tools, driver support, device capability, or account permissions can leave a metric, a chart option, or a GPU control unavailable. **A visible GPU does not imply that power, clock, memory-clock, or fan changes are supported.**

Use the Hardware page as the host-specific answer. For capacity decisions, combine its live memory and storage data with the requirements of the model and plugin you plan to use.

### Hardware monitoring [page: hardware-monitoring]

The **Hardware** page combines the current host snapshot with stored history for the devices and metrics that SoAI can collect. It is the place to check CPU, memory, storage, network, and GPU behavior while a model or plugin is running.

This page is the manual view. A model can read a live host snapshot through the `hardware_snapshot` agent tool, then use SoAI's two internal hardware tools to act on the result. See [Monitor from an agent](#agent-monitoring) below and [Hardware tools](#hardware-tools).

#### Open the Hardware page

1. In the SoAI WebUI, open **Hardware** from the side navigation.
2. Review the live cards for the host's CPU, memory, storage, network interfaces, and detected GPUs.
3. Use **Info** in the page header when you need the host information view.
4. Use **Logs** to continue investigating a problem in the logs page. That page requires **Log access** ( [`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS) ).

The page requires **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)). A Standard user does not receive that permission by default. The process card appears only with **Process viewing** ([`HW_PROCESS_VIEW`](#acl-HW_PROCESS_VIEW)), and GPU controls have their own **GPU tuning** ([`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING)) requirement. **Missing data means that SoAI did not receive that metric for the current device and host state (it is not a zero measurement).**

A mixed-vendor host can show [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/), [AMD](https://www.amd.com/), and [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) cards together. SoAI probes every detected vendor and keeps device identities distinct across vendors. Detailed [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) telemetry requires `amd-smi` on [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/); detailed [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) telemetry requires `xpu-smi` on [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) or `xpu-smi.exe` on [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/); and detailed [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) telemetry requires the vendor driver and [NVML](https://developer.nvidia.com/management-library-nvml) or `nvidia-smi` path.

#### Use charts, sampling, and comparisons

1. In **Chart**, choose a **Device**.
2. Choose a **Metric** that the selected device reports.
3. Choose the time range and chart type you need.
4. When using the **OHLC** chart type, use **Interval** to choose the aggregation interval.

The available devices, metrics, time ranges, and intervals come from the current hardware snapshot and history capability data. If history is disabled, Chart shows **History is disabled by the backend.** Select **Export** in the page header after selecting the hardware source you want to export. SoAI opens an export preview for that source.

##### Change sampling and retention

The **Advanced** control in Settings appears only to an Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)). Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu. Select **Advanced** in the page header, choose the **System** tab, and open the **Hardware** group. Change **Monitoring interval ms**, **Hardware history enabled**, or **Db retention hours**, then select **Save**. If Settings shows the **Restart SoAI** action, use it when you are ready to apply the pending restart.

The factory defaults sample every 3000 milliseconds, enable history, and retain hardware history for 168 hours. Their current values, defaults, and restart requirements are listed in [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS), [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED), and [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DB_RETENTION_HOURS`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DB_RETENTION_HOURS).

##### Compare a change

Keep the model, plugin, prompt shape, concurrency, selected device, and time window consistent while comparing a change. Read temperature, power, utilization, memory use, and plugin behavior together. **One metric on its own does not establish the cause of a slowdown or failure.**

#### Monitor from an agent

`hardware_snapshot` returns the same live readings this page shows. Left unset it reports uptime, OS, CPU, memory, and GPU; its `components` argument adds storage, network, swap, motherboard, and measured disk and network speed. `include_processes` adds the per-GPU process list and requires an administrator, the same distinction the process card makes here. The tool reads the live snapshot only. Stored history, the **Chart** time ranges, and **Export** stay on this page.

A WebUI conversation needs a model that supports tool calling, **MCP usage** ([`MCP_USE`](#acl-MCP_USE)), and `hardware_snapshot` selected under **Chat configuration > Tools**. **The tool requires an authenticated user context but does not check the Hardware page's [`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ) permission.** `include_processes=true` also requires an Administrator.

Monitoring that should act on what it reads pairs it with `hardware_control` and `hardware_benchmark`: read a baseline, change one GPU setting, then stress-test the result. Those two are administrator-only, **Execute mode** only, and internal to SoAI. They belong to the administrator catalog, so MCP server mode never publishes them to third-party software that uses SoAI as an MCP server, which can read a snapshot but cannot change or stress a GPU. [GPU controls and tuning](#gpu-controls-and-tuning) covers the manual equivalent of that loop, and [Hardware tools](#hardware-tools) covers all three tools.

### GPU controls and tuning [page: gpu-controls-and-tuning]

**SoAI exposes a GPU slider only when the current GPU, driver, and vendor backend report that control as actionable.** Monitoring remains available when a device has no supported hardware changes.

For manual control in the SoAI WebUI, open **Hardware** and change a setting yourself. The same power, clock, and fan settings are also reachable by a model through the hardware agent tools, described in [Hardware tools](#hardware-tools). See [Let a model apply the settings](#agent-control) below for when to choose which.

#### Control availability and measurement

Open **Hardware** from the side navigation. The page itself requires **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)). The **GPU control** section appears only to an Administrator with **GPU tuning** ([`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING)). If no detected GPU reports an actionable control, the section shows **No GPU controls available**. Standard users cannot receive that permission.

A panel can offer **Power limit**, **Core clock offset**, **Memory clock offset**, or **Fan speed**. Each slider appears separately, so an absent control is unavailable for that GPU in its current host state.

The global [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HARDWARE_MUTATION_DISABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HARDWARE_MUTATION_DISABLED) setting prevents hardware mutations. SoAI rejects mutation requests while it is enabled. An Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) can select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu. Select **Advanced** in the page header and search for the complete configuration path. Set **Hardware mutation disabled** to Off, then select **Save**.

What a slider does depends on the vendor backend behind it. An [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) card takes a power limit in watts and clock offsets in MHz through [NVML](https://developer.nvidia.com/management-library-nvml), while [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) applies power and fan through `amd-smi` and reaches clocks through performance levels or the AMDGPU OverDrive files, so a raw MHz offset is not always what you get. [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) exposes a power limit and a clamped core-clock range through `xpu-smi` and has no fan or memory clock control at all. The [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) and [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) paths act on host interfaces that need elevated privileges, so a control can be listed and still fail because the host refuses the change. SoAI clamps a requested value into the range the device reports, and a change the backend cannot perform comes back as an explicit failure rather than a silent no-op.

##### Measure before tuning

1. In **Hardware > Chart**, select the GPU and the metrics that matter to the workload, such as utilization, temperature, power draw, and memory use.
2. Run the model with the same prompt shape and concurrency you intend to compare later.
3. Record the result before changing a hardware setting.

**There is no universally safe or faster power, clock, or fan value.** Driver limits, cooling, GPU firmware, model size, backend, and workload all affect the result. Keep only a change that improves the workload you measured without exceeding the operating limits of the hardware.

#### Risk, warranty, and where to start

**The GPU control panel carries a standing warning that incorrect settings may damage your GPU, and it is meant literally.** Raising clocks moves the card outside the operating point its manufacturer validated, and the cost is paid in heat, current, and stability: crashes and driver resets are the visible failures, while accelerated wear is the one you notice a year later. Warranty terms differ by vendor and by board partner, and some cover tuning done with the vendor's own utility while others do not, with the [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) warranty excluding damage caused by overclocking even when [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) hardware or software performed it. Read the terms that came with your card before you raise anything, and treat a dead card as a real possible cost of the experiment rather than a remote one.

Lowering the power limit is the opposite trade, and it is the one most local inference hosts actually want. Token generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than by core clock, so a card held under its stock power ceiling keeps most of its throughput while drawing noticeably less: published measurements on machine-learning hosts put a cut of 10% to 20% at roughly 95% of full performance, and deeper cuts on high-end consumer cards trade a few percent of tokens per second for a large drop in watts. The result is a cooler, quieter card, less thermal cycling over a long run, and less strain on the host power supply and the circuit it is plugged into, which is why multi-GPU builds are often configured this way on purpose instead of as a fallback. Sustained heat is the main thing that ages a card running inference for hours at a time, so a lower ceiling is a longevity argument as much as an electricity one, and nothing about it is permanent because setting the control back to **Auto** restores stock behavior.

Memory clock deserves its own caution. GPU memory errors do not announce themselves: the card corrects or replays what it can and passes the rest through, so a memory overclock that looks stable in a game surfaces in inference as wrong output rather than as a crash. Raise it in small steps if you raise it at all, keep a prompt whose good answer you already know, and back off at the first inconsistent result instead of waiting for a visible artifact.

The rest is ordinary discipline. Change one control at a time so a failure has one candidate cause, move in small increments, and rerun the same workload after each change, because a setting that helps one measurement can hurt another. Instability from clocks often appears only once the card has been hot for a while, so a long run tells you more than a short one, and it is worth writing down the last setting that survived it. Manual fan speed is the quiet exception in this list: fixing a percentage removes the driver's own temperature response, and a value that is comfortable at idle can be far too low an hour into a sustained load.

#### Apply, test, and save settings

1. Find the GPU's **GPU control** panel.
2. For a supported setting, turn off **Auto** and set a value within the displayed range.
3. Select **Apply**.
4. Use the live telemetry and **Chart** to check the result before changing another control.

**Reset** returns supported power and fan controls to **Auto** and resets supported clock controls, and it does not remove a saved slot.

##### Test the result

1. After applying a setting, select **Test**.
2. Select **Bench** for a certified SoAIBench run, or **Stress** for a stability run.
3. Watch temperature, power, and status while it runs, and select **Stop** to end a stress run early.
4. After a run exists, use the **History** control in the GPU panel to compare or export previous results.

A stress run started from this page lasts at most 60 seconds and ends on its own, so **Stop** only shortens it. That run has no temperature limit either: a certified **Bench** run aborts when the card passes 100 C, while the stress profile stops when it finishes, when you stop it, or when the card gives out. Watch the temperature yourself during a stress run, or start the run through `hardware_benchmark` with an explicit `temperature_limit_celsius`, which is the only way to set one. The benchmark controls report an explicit unsupported result when the selected GPU or runtime cannot run the requested profile, and a host whose cooling, power delivery, or operating limits are unknown is not a host to stress-test.

##### Save and reuse a slot

1. Apply and test a manual setting.
2. Select **Save**, then select slot **1**, **2**, or **3**.
3. To reuse a saved setting, select its filled slot to preview it, then select **Apply**.
4. With a saved slot selected, choose **Apply at boot** and select **Apply** to make that slot the startup profile.

**Apply at boot** is shown only while a saved slot is selected, and saving new values into a slot replaces that slot's settings. The boot flag survives a clean restart but deliberately does not survive a crash: when SoAI starts after an unclean shutdown it clears **Apply at boot** on every saved device, so a profile that may have contributed to the hang is not reapplied on the way back up. Re-enable it once you are satisfied the host is stable, and recheck a saved profile after a GPU or driver change before relying on it at startup.

That start also returns power, fan, and clock control to safe defaults, so an applied profile is gone as well as the boot flag, and it is not the only recovery work an unclean shutdown causes: the same start verifies the core database before SoAI serves anything, which can hold up startup for minutes and should not be interrupted. [After an unclean shutdown](#after-an-unclean-shutdown) covers both, which is worth reading before a session of overclocking that may hang the host more than once.

#### Let a model apply the settings

An agent reaches the same controls through three tools. `hardware_snapshot` reads the sensors and reports the GPU device IDs, `hardware_control` lists the supported controls for a card and applies power, fan, and clock values, and `hardware_benchmark` runs a stress or SoAIBench workload to check the result. [Hardware tools](#hardware-tools) covers their arguments and the order to use them in.

A conversation needs a model that supports tool calling, the **MCP usage** ([`MCP_USE`](#acl-MCP_USE)) permission, and the tools selected in **Chat configuration > Tools**. `hardware_control` and `hardware_benchmark` also require an administrator and **Execute mode**, and they refuse to run outside a live agent turn that selected them. **Chat and Plan mode cannot reach them at all.**

Those two tools are internal to SoAI. They belong to the administrator catalog only, so they never appear in the tool list that MCP server mode publishes. Third-party software that uses SoAI as an MCP server can call `hardware_snapshot` but cannot change or stress a GPU. Model-orchestrated GPU control happens inside a SoAI conversation or not at all.

Use this page for a one-off change you want to see and confirm yourself, including saved slots and **Apply at boot**, which the tools do not manage. Use the tools when a reading should lead to a change and a follow-up benchmark without you driving each step. Leave **Require tool approval** on for any conversation that can reach them, so you still see the exact settings before SoAI applies them.

### GPU setup and troubleshooting [page: gpu-setup-and-troubleshooting]

In the SoAI WebUI, start with the **Hardware** page. It shows the values SoAI can receive from the host, its driver, and the vendor tools. A GPU can be detected while some telemetry or controls remain unavailable, so identify the missing capability before changing the host.

#### Check access and the reported state

1. Open **Hardware** from the side navigation.
2. Review the GPU card, then select that GPU in **Chart** if you need its stored history.
3. Check whether the **GPU control** panel is present and which controls it contains.

The page requires **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)). To grant it to a Standard user, an Administrator with **ACL administration** ([`ACL_ADMIN`](#acl-ACL_ADMIN)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then selects **Settings** from its menu and **ACL**. Open the **Standard user** group, enable **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)), and select **Save**. The GPU control panel needs **GPU tuning** ([`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING)) as well, and that one is not merely off by default for Standard users: the Standard group cannot hold it at all, so an account that needs GPU control needs to be an Administrator.

#### Check the vendor tool and driver

SoAI identifies GPUs before any vendor tool answers, so a card can appear on the page with very little attached to it. On [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) that first pass is a PCI scan, and on [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) it is a WMI query of the display adapters, with vendor telemetry merged onto that list afterwards. A GPU without telemetry reports why: usually the vendor tool is missing, while an [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) card bound to a kernel driver other than the [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) one reports instead that the driver is inactive. A tool that is installed but denied permission, and a tool that times out, both look the same as a missing tool, so run the tool yourself as the account SoAI runs under before concluding it is absent.

| Vendor | Current collection path | What an unavailable result means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) | `amd-smi` on [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/). | Without `amd-smi`, SoAI cannot collect [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) telemetry or expose [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) controls. This path is [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) only, so an [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) card on [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) is listed by name with neither. |
| [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) | `xpu-smi` on [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) or `xpu-smi.exe` on [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/). | Without the matching tool, SoAI cannot collect [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) telemetry or expose [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) controls. |
| [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) | [NVML](https://developer.nvidia.com/management-library-nvml) when available, with an `nvidia-smi` query path when [NVML](https://developer.nvidia.com/management-library-nvml) is unavailable. | Check that the [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) driver is installed and running, then refresh Hardware. |

A vendor tool does not make every setting available, and the Hardware page renders only the controls that the current device reports as supported. Part of [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) clock control also goes through the AMDGPU OverDrive files under `/sys/class/drm` rather than through `amd-smi`, which is why an [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) control can appear on a host whose `amd-smi` telemetry is thin, and why [AMD](https://www.amd.com/) and [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) changes can still fail on a host that does not grant the privileges those interfaces need. [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) has no GPU collection path at all today, so the Hardware page lists no GPU there even on a machine that has one.

**Readings are cached, so a fix does not show up the moment you make it.** The GPU snapshot is held for 1 second ([`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.GPU_INFO_CACHE_TTL_SEC`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.GPU_INFO_CACHE_TTL_SEC)), the rest of the host snapshot for 2 seconds ([`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_CACHE_TTL`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_CACHE_TTL)), and the vendor detection that decides which vendor tools are worth querying is held for 60 seconds ([`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.GPU_VENDOR_CACHE_TTL_SEC`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.GPU_VENDOR_CACHE_TTL_SEC)). Give the page a minute after installing `amd-smi`, `xpu-smi`, or a driver before deciding the install changed nothing. In the other direction, a probe that returns no GPUs while a GPU vendor is still detected on the host keeps the last inventory that had one rather than blanking the page, so a card that was genuinely removed or hidden can linger until a later probe succeeds.

#### Install a driver on SoAI OS

Open the **Settings** menu at the right of the header, select **Settings**, then **Drivers**. This tab is available only on SoAI OS to an Administrator with **SoAI OS administration** ([`HOST_MANAGEMENT_ADMIN`](#acl-HOST_MANAGEMENT_ADMIN)). Follow [SoAI OS GPU drivers](#soai-os-gpu-drivers) for detection, preview, installation, and reboot guidance instead of changing host packages outside that workflow.

The [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) plan installs the graphics firmware, the Mesa drivers, and `intel-gpu-tools`, and it does not install `xpu-smi`, which is not available as a native [Debian](https://www.debian.org/) 13 package through SoAI OS. **[Intel](https://www.intel.com/) telemetry and [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) controls therefore stay unavailable after a successful [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) driver install until you supply that tool yourself.**

#### Controls are missing or rejected

A visible GPU is not enough for a hardware change. The signed-in account needs **GPU tuning** ([`HW_GPU_TUNING`](#acl-HW_GPU_TUNING)), the device must report the control, and the vendor backend must remain available. If a control disappears after a driver change, return to Hardware and inspect the current capability set instead of reusing an old value.

SoAI rejects hardware mutations while [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HARDWARE_MUTATION_DISABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.HARDWARE_MUTATION_DISABLED) is enabled. An Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) can select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then select **Settings** from its menu. Select **Advanced** in the page header, search for the complete configuration path, set **Hardware mutation disabled** to Off, and select **Save**.

**A container looks the same as a missing driver.** SoAI reads the hardware its own process can see, so a container started without GPU passthrough shows the card with no telemetry or does not list it at all, with nothing on the page to separate that from an uninstalled driver. Check passthrough on the host before reinstalling anything inside the container.

## Security

### Security hardening [page: security-hardening]

SoAI is a management plane for models, accounts, files, tools, and host resources. **Its security controls reduce common web, credential, and tool-exposure risks, but they do not turn the service into a safe public internet endpoint.** Run SoAI on the local machine or behind a private network boundary. For remote access, prefer an authenticated VPN, such as a [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com/) tunnel or a comparable private-network service.

#### Security boundaries

| Boundary | What SoAI enforces | Operator responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts and credentials | WebUI sessions, inference API keys, and MCP tokens use separate authentication paths. ACL actions limit administrative and tool access. | Give each person or client its own credential, grant the smallest useful permission set, set expirations, and revoke access that is no longer needed. See [Passwords and credential tools](#passwords-and-credential-tools) for password and vault guidance. |
| Browser requests | SoAI validates CSRF tokens for unsafe cookie-authenticated requests and rejects unsafe cross-site cookie requests. Origin policy also protects WebSocket and MCP browser connections. | Keep allowed origins narrow and protect browser sessions from untrusted extensions, scripts, and devices. |
| Network transport | SoAI supports TLS, secure-cookie policy, trusted proxy networks, CORS policy, rate limits, and configurable bind addresses. | Use a firewall or VPN as the main network boundary. Configure TLS and proxy trust for the path clients use. |
| Tools and code | ACL checks, feature switches, MCP exposure lists, workspace roots, and private-network egress checks limit specific capabilities. | Treat tools and plugins according to their impact. Some run with the operating-system permissions of the SoAI process and are not sandboxed. |

These controls work together. Authentication does not make a dangerous tool harmless, TLS does not reduce the privileges carried by a stolen token, and a reverse proxy does not isolate the SoAI process from its host.

#### Built-in protections

SoAI applies several controls before an ACL-protected operation or tool runs. Each control covers a specific part of the request or runtime:

| Control | Enforced behavior | Scope and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authentication lifecycle | Normal application routes stay unavailable until the first administrator completes setup. Creating the first API-key record makes bearer authentication mandatory on compatible inference APIs. | After setup, compatible inference APIs remain unauthenticated while the API-key store has no records. [Authentication and API keys](#authentication-and-api-keys) explains this state transition. |
| Credentials and sessions | WebUI passwords use [Argon2](https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2) hashes. SoAI stores inference API keys and MCP personal access tokens as salted HMAC-derived values and fingerprints after showing each secret once. Persisted linked-account and MCP server secrets use encryption tied to the installation key. | WebUI sessions expire and can be [revoked by device or by account](#users-roles-and-sessions). A password change invalidates the account's earlier sessions. Protect the installation key and its backups because they are part of the [password and credential boundary](#passwords-and-credential-tools). |
| Browser requests and responses | Session cookies are HttpOnly and `SameSite=Lax`. SoAI validates CSRF tokens on unsafe cookie-authenticated requests and checks cross-site request metadata plus WebSocket and MCP connection origins. Responses carry content security, anti-framing, MIME-sniffing, referrer, resource, and browser-permission headers. | HSTS is sent only for HTTPS requests when enabled. These controls protect the SoAI browser interface; they cannot secure a compromised browser profile, extension, or client device. |
| Network admission | Client-address access rules can reject a request before route handling. Secure-transport policy can reject or redirect plain HTTP. SoAI accepts proxy-derived client and scheme headers only from configured proxy networks. | These application checks supplement the host firewall and VPN. They do not replace either boundary. |
| Resource bounds | HTTP request bodies have separate native and compatible-API size ceilings plus a read deadline. Tool families add response, upload, snapshot, script, concurrency, and timeout limits. | The bounds reduce memory, oversized-input, and slow-request abuse. They do not authorize a request or guarantee enough capacity for accepted work. |
| Outbound requests | Browser navigation blocks private and loopback destinations while SoAI is online. Other network tools have separate private-network egress switches. | The defaults differ by tool. Review each enabled network capability before an agent processes untrusted content. |
| Plugin admission | SoAI checks plugin package structure, hashes, dependencies, and compatibility before launch. Default-on [`PLUGINS.SECURITY.SAFETY_VALIDATION`](#config-PLUGINS.SECURITY.SAFETY_VALIDATION) adds static source and import checks. | Admission rejects known-invalid packages. It cannot prove that third-party code is trustworthy, and plugin workers do not provide an operating-system sandbox. |
| Audit logging | The audit log records actors, anonymized client addresses, actions, targets, and sanitized details for events such as ACL denials, API-key changes, configuration mutations, terminal sessions, file operations, and plugin changes. | Audit records support review and incident response after an event. They do not prevent the recorded action. |

#### Factory defaults are a starting point

The default SoAI configuration is an operational starting point, not the most restrictive configuration or the recommended final state for an installation that needs stronger security. No single hardened profile fits a local workstation, a shared LAN service, a VPN-only deployment, and an installation with external integrations. Tailor the configuration to the people, clients, networks, data, models, and tools that the instance must serve, and always disable or restrict capabilities that are not required. Resetting to factory defaults is not a hardening action.

**Hardening reduces available functionality.** Completing the hardening appropriate to a deployment can mean losing access to some SoAI features, such as remote discovery, shell and terminal access, private-network requests, persistent browser sessions, or externally exposed MCP tools. That loss of capability is intentional: each unavailable path is also a path that an unauthorized user, compromised client, unsafe plugin, or prompt-injected model cannot use.

Start with [Network and TLS](#network-and-tls), which documents the default listener behavior and transport settings, then complete the [hardening checklist below](#hardening-checklist). Run the WebUI security hardening audit after setup and after meaningful network, access, tool, plugin, or integration changes. Resolve each applicable finding according to the deployment rather than assuming that a shipped default is the safest value for that environment.

#### Rate limits and quotas

SoAI has separate controls for authentication failures, request frequency, and API-key consumption. WebUI login failures use separate buckets for the client address, the address and username pair, and the username. The default permits 10 failures in 300 seconds, configured by [`SERVER.WEBUI.LOGIN_SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.MAX_FAILURES`](#config-SERVER.WEBUI.LOGIN_SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.MAX_FAILURES) and [`SERVER.WEBUI.LOGIN_SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.WINDOW_SECONDS`](#config-SERVER.WEBUI.LOGIN_SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.WINDOW_SECONDS). Invalid bearer authentication on compatible inference APIs uses client-address and token-fingerprint buckets. Its defaults are five failures in 60 seconds, controlled by [`API.OPENAI.SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.MAX_FAILURES`](#config-API.OPENAI.SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.MAX_FAILURES) and [`API.OPENAI.SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.WINDOW_SECONDS`](#config-API.OPENAI.SECURITY.AUTH_FAILURE_RATELIMIT.WINDOW_SECONDS). A blocked attempt returns `429` with retry guidance.

**General API request limiting is controlled by [`API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.ENABLED`](#config-API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.ENABLED) and is disabled by default.** On a network-exposed deployment, the security hardening audit reports that disabled state. When enabled, SoAI creates a moving-window bucket for each remote client address and configured route path across registered native, MCP, OpenAI-compatible, and Anthropic-compatible routes. The default for non-streaming routes, [`API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.DEFAULT_LIMIT`](#config-API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.DEFAULT_LIMIT) is `600/minute`, while [`API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.STREAM_LIMIT`](#config-API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.STREAM_LIMIT) is `60/minute`. Use [`API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.ROUTERS`](#config-API.OPENAI.RATE_LIMITING.ROUTERS) for router and path-specific policy. Trusted proxy configuration must be correct for SoAI to identify the real client address. The counters live in the running API process and reset after a process restart or a change to the rate-limit rules.

API-key quotas are a different control. They cap requests or tokens over hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly windows for one key or its assigned WebUI user. A quota does not smooth bursts, and request rate limiting does not enforce a usage budget. Use both where several clients share an instance. Neither replaces ACL, authentication, model concurrency limits, a firewall, or a private network boundary.

#### Prompt injection and untrusted content

Prompt injection is text in a webpage, document, email, code file, retrieved knowledge, or tool result that tries to redirect the model away from the user's request. The dedicated [SoAI system prompt](#soai-system-prompt) page shows the built-in prompt, when SoAI adds it, and how it is prepared for each turn. When that prompt is enabled, it tells the model to treat instructions embedded in user-provided content as data, to treat tool results and external content as untrusted, and to use only the tools SoAI lists in the runtime tool context. Attached content remains separate from SoAI's runtime-owned system and tool context.

SoAI also limits what a successful injection can reach outside the model. Account ACL, runtime policy, and the conversation's mode-specific tool selection determine which tools are available. Plan mode blocks destructive tools and tools without valid destructive metadata. When **Require tool approval** is enabled, SoAI pauses covered calls and shows the proposed tool input before the user approves or denies execution. These checks are enforced by SoAI rather than left to the model's judgment. In conversations that process untrusted content, approve one call at a time instead of remembering the approval for later calls.

Keep shell tools disabled when an agent does not need to run host commands. Set [`TOOLS.MCP.SHELL.ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SHELL.ENABLED) to `false`, leave shell tools out of the conversation's selected tools, and do not grant **Terminal and shell access** ([`TERMINAL_USE`](#acl-TERMINAL_USE)) to accounts that do not need it. Disabling shell does not prevent prompt injection itself, but it removes a high-impact path an injected model could use to execute commands with the SoAI process's host permissions. A command blacklist is not a security boundary. See [File and shell tools](#file-and-shell-tools) for the installation switch, account permission, and execution boundary.

When an agent can use saved credentials or secret handles, also disable browser JavaScript evaluation unless the task specifically needs it. **`browser_eval` is enabled by default and can read a password after an autofill tool places it in the page.** Set [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED) to `false` and leave `browser_eval` out of the selected tools. See [Passwords and credential tools](#passwords-and-credential-tools) for the complete credential boundary.

These measures reduce risk; they do not guarantee that a model will recognize or refuse every hostile instruction. Smaller models and models with weaker instruction following are generally more likely to be diverted, but larger models are not exempt and model size is not a security boundary. Treat user-authored system prompts and workspace instruction files such as `SOAI.md` or `AGENTS.md` as trusted configuration, because SoAI intentionally provides them to the agent as instructions. No model choice or prompt makes untrusted content safe by itself; choose the model and its available authority accordingly. See [Agent mode, tool approvals, and checkpoints](#agent-mode-tool-approvals-and-checkpoints) for mode and approval behavior.

#### Browser ad blocking

Browser ad blocking is enabled by default through [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.BLOCK_ADS`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.BLOCK_ADS). SoAI intercepts [Chromium](https://www.chromium.org/) network requests and applies [EasyList](https://easylist.to/) rules with request type, document origin, and first-party or third-party context. It starts with a packaged rule set, refreshes it from the configured source, and retains the existing matcher if a refresh fails. Blocking known advertising requests reduces exposure to third-party ad content and malicious advertising while also lowering page noise and resource use.

Ad blocking is defense in depth, not page isolation. [EasyList](https://easylist.to/) cannot identify every hostile script, tracking request, compromised first-party resource, prompt injection, or unsafe user action. It does not replace the browser's private-network navigation policy, a separate browser profile, least-privilege tools, or human review of consequential actions. See [Browser automation tools](#browser-automation-tools) for browser configuration and authority boundaries.

Browser-backed rendering used by web extraction has its own default-on control, [`TOOLS.RAG.WEB.BROWSER_RENDER_BLOCK_ADS`](#config-TOOLS.RAG.WEB.BROWSER_RENDER_BLOCK_ADS). The security hardening audit reports a disabled ad-blocking control when the corresponding browser capability is enabled.

#### Recommended deployment boundary

Keep the WebUI, System API, compatible inference APIs, MCP endpoint, and discovery service off the public internet. A TLS reverse proxy can terminate certificates, apply request limits, and route WebSocket traffic, but it still forwards accepted requests to SoAI. It does not remove application vulnerabilities, compromised credentials, prompt injection, or the host impact of server-side tools. **SoAI does not recommend direct internet exposure, even when a reverse proxy sits in front of it.**

Use `localhost` for a single-machine installation. For access from another trusted device, place both devices on a controlled LAN or connect them through an authenticated VPN. [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com/) and services built on the same private overlay model are suitable examples. Restrict the host firewall and bind addresses to that private path, keep the discovery service private, and use TLS when traffic crosses a network you do not control. See [Network and TLS](#network-and-tls) for the transport settings.

#### Security hardening audit in the SoAI WebUI

An administrator with Configuration changes ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) and ACL administration ([`ACL_ADMIN`](#acl-ACL_ADMIN)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, selects **Settings** from its menu, then opens **Security**. The **Security hardening audit** evaluates the persisted Core configuration, user workspace placement, active administrator device sessions, API keys, and MCP access tokens. Each finding includes a stable issue ID and an explanation, plus configuration or workspace references when they apply. The page presents flagged configuration fields as recommended actions and links workspace findings to **Users**.

The audit checks network exposure, transport and cookie policy, CORS and trusted proxies, API authentication and rate limiting, logging, terminal and tool access, private-network egress, browser protections, plugin security, MCP server exposure, credential expiration, administrator sessions, and unsafe workspace relationships to the SoAI installation. **Some findings apply only when the affected capability is enabled or the deployment is reachable beyond the local machine.** The set of checks follows the running SoAI version, so use the report itself as the source for the findings on that instance.

#### Security hardening findings in backend logs

Before the API and WebUI server starts, SoAI runs the same security audit using the loaded Core configuration. The startup audit includes workspace placement, administrator device sessions, API keys, and MCP access tokens. If it finds an issue, the Core log receives a warning beginning with `Security hardening: N issue(s) detected`. The warning lists each issue ID and message, followed by any applicable configuration or workspace references. Open **Logs** from the **Settings** menu at the right of the header, select the Core source, and search the startup entries for `Security hardening`. A sidebar link is available only after the user adds Logs under **Settings > Theme > Sidebar**. Access to Logs requires Log access ([`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS)).

The configured log location comes from [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOGS_PATH) and [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.MAIN_LOG). SoAI writes the startup security warning only when it finds an issue.

#### What a green result means

A green result means that the checks implemented by the running version found no issue in the state they inspected. **It is a configuration audit, not a penetration test or a guarantee that the deployment is safe.** It does not verify the external firewall, VPN, reverse proxy, DNS, client devices, credential storage, third-party plugins, model behavior, or every prompt-injection path. A green result does not make public internet exposure a recommended deployment.

Treat a finding as a concrete action, then decide whether the affected capability should remain enabled at all. Treat a green result as one input to the deployment review. Continue to use private network access, least privilege, individual credentials, current software, trusted plugins, backups, and host-level isolation appropriate to the data and tools the instance can reach.

#### Protect backups and the installation key

A managed backup includes the primary database, Core configuration, installation encryption key, plugin sidecar configuration, user data, and saved GPU settings by default. **A downloaded `.tar.gz` archive is not an encrypted backup format.** Anyone who obtains the archive may gain access to account data, workspace files, provider credentials, and the key needed to decrypt stored secrets. Protect backup files with the same care as the running instance and keep recovery copies outside the SoAI host on access-controlled storage.

The WebUI **Verify** action checks the managed backup's manifest and recorded contents. A **Valid** result does not mean that the archive is encrypted, safe to share, or stored in a suitable disaster-recovery location. Review [Backup](#backup) and [Restore](#restore) before relying on a recovery point.

#### High-impact tools and plugins

**MCP tools execute on the SoAI server.** Shell commands inherit the operating-system identity of the SoAI process, and MCP shell calls do not pause for the WebUI approval dialog. Server-side file tools reach the token owner's workspace. Browser tools block private-network destinations, but they can still use saved web sessions, upload workspace files, and act on public sites. Linked-account, vault, automation, subagent, persistent-mutation, and resource-intensive tools carry their own data, account, or capacity risks.

Keep high-impact tools out of MCP server mode unless a trusted local client needs them. A suitable case is a local coding agent connected to a local SoAI instance on the same controlled machine. Do not expose these tools to a remote MCP client. A local connection remains unsafe if its model, prompts, repository, browsed content, or other inputs can contain hostile instructions. Review [MCP overview](#mcp-overview) and [File and shell tools](#file-and-shell-tools) before enabling them.

Plugin workers separate plugin lifecycle state from the main process, but they do not provide an operating-system sandbox. Install plugins only from a source you trust. On SoAI OS, host-management permissions can reach the root-owned management service, so review the [SoAI OS security model](#soai-os-security-model) as well.

#### Hardening checklist

Work through this checklist before relying on a SoAI instance. It applies to SoAI Core and SoAI OS; host controls increase the consequence of a compromised administrator session.

##### Accounts and credentials

1. Complete the setup wizard with a long, unique administrator password and store it in a separate password manager. See [Passwords and credential tools](#passwords-and-credential-tools).
2. Open **Settings > Users**, give administrator access only to operators who need it, and review users after staffing changes. This tab requires **User administration** ( [`USER_ADMIN`](#acl-USER_ADMIN) ).
3. Open **Settings > [OpenAI](https://openai.com/)**. In **[OpenAI](https://openai.com/) server API keys**, create a separate key for each client, choose an expiration, and revoke the key when that client leaves service. This tab requires **API key management** ( [`OPENAI_API_ADMIN`](#acl-OPENAI_API_ADMIN) ).
4. Store each key outside source control. The WebUI shows its plaintext only when SoAI creates it.

##### Network and transport

1. Choose a local, LAN, or VPN-only boundary, then restrict the host firewall and bind addresses to it.
2. Enable TLS with a certificate clients can validate. Test the complete WebUI and API path before enforcing redirects or HSTS.
3. Replace broad CORS settings with explicit browser origins and preserve WebSocket upgrades at a reverse proxy.
4. Keep the discovery port off untrusted networks. Discovery helps the WebUI locate the API but does not replace authentication.

##### Tools and host access

1. Open **Settings > MCP > MCP configuration > Server mode**. Set **Exposed tools**, **Exposed resources**, and **Exposed prompts** to only what each client needs, then limit **Allowed origins** to trusted client origins. These controls require **MCP administration** ( [`MCP_ADMIN`](#acl-MCP_ADMIN) ) and **Configuration changes** ( [`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH) ).
2. Keep shell, server-side file access, browser sessions, linked accounts, vault access, automations, subagents, arbitrary HTTP methods, and other persistent or resource-intensive tools out of [`TOOLS.MCP.SERVER_MODE.EXPOSED_TOOLS`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SERVER_MODE.EXPOSED_TOOLS) unless a trusted client specifically needs them. The defaults exclude these high-impact families, and the security audit flags explicit opt-ins on a network-exposed deployment.
3. Use high-impact MCP tools only for a trusted local client connected to a local SoAI instance. Treat even a same-host client as untrusted when its model, prompts, repository, browsed content, or other inputs can contain hostile instructions.
4. Disable MCP shell and WebUI terminal access unless operators understand the host impact. MCP shell is controlled by [`TOOLS.MCP.SHELL.ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SHELL.ENABLED), and the WebUI terminal is controlled by [`SERVER.WEBUI.TERMINAL.ENABLED`](#config-SERVER.WEBUI.TERMINAL.ENABLED). A command blacklist is not a security boundary.
5. Disable [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED) when browser sessions handle credentials and JavaScript evaluation is not required. The structured typing tool blocks password and one-time-code fields, but arbitrary page JavaScript can read their values after autofill.
6. On SoAI OS, review **SoAI OS administration** ( [`HOST_MANAGEMENT_ADMIN`](#acl-HOST_MANAGEMENT_ADMIN) ) separately from ordinary WebUI access because it authorizes privileged actions through the root-owned management service.
7. On SoAI OS, keep network safe-apply, SSH recovery, and local-console access available before changing remote access.

##### Audit and recovery readiness

1. Open **Settings > Security** and resolve every hardening finding that applies to the deployment.
2. Check the Core startup log after configuration, workspace, network, plugin, or upgrade changes.
3. Schedule backups and rehearse a restore using the data and configuration you expect to recover.
4. Keep enough disk space for model downloads, backups, package updates, and temporary files.
5. Read task results and audit events after driver, storage, update, network, or user changes. Do not treat an accepted task as a completed task.
6. Keep [Operational runbooks](#operational-runbooks), [Authentication and API keys](#authentication-and-api-keys), and [Network and TLS](#network-and-tls) with the operator handoff.

### Access control [page: access-control]

SoAI uses a role-based access control list (ACL) to decide which authenticated accounts may use administrative, model, tool, file, hardware, and system capabilities. Each account has either the **Administrator** or **Regular user** role; the ACL page calls the latter **Standard user**. **The policy assigns actions to roles, so changing a Standard user permission changes it for every Regular user account.** Use **Users** to change one account's role and **ACL** to change what each role can do.

#### Manage role permissions

An administrator with **ACL administration** (`ACL_ADMIN`) opens **Settings > ACL**. Expand **Administrator** or **Standard user**, change the available toggles, then select **Save**. The security policy fixes disabled controls, and the Bootstrap and Anonymous roles are immutable. To discard every override, open **Reset**, find **ACL policy**, and select **Reset** after reading the confirmation.

Administrators start with every action. The reference marks the initial Standard user actions as **Standard: default**. An ACL administrator can enable entries marked **Standard: optional**. **Administrator-only actions cannot be granted to the Standard role.** ACL administration, licensing administration, and recovery administration cannot be removed from the Administrator role.

#### Permission reference

| Permission | Action ID | Allows | Availability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ACL administration | `ACL_ADMIN` | Modify access control policies. | Administrator only; required |
| API key management | `OPENAI_API_ADMIN` | Manage compatible inference API keys. | Administrator only |
| Backup administration | `BACKUP_ADMIN` | Create, restore, and delete backups. | Administrator only |
| Bootstrap setup access | `WIZARD_BOOTSTRAP` | Access the setup surface before the first account and normal ACL state exist. | Bootstrap only; fixed |
| Configuration changes | `CONFIG_PATCH` | Modify Core configuration settings. | Administrator only |
| Factory reset | `FACTORY_RESET` | Reset the system to factory defaults. | Administrator only |
| Files administration | `FILE_EXPLORER_ADMIN` | Perform privileged file operations. | Administrator only |

### Authentication and API keys [page: authentication-and-api-keys]

People sign in to the WebUI with a browser session, covered in [Users, roles, and sessions](#users-roles-and-sessions). Applications use API keys for SoAI's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible API surfaces. MCP clients use separate personal access tokens; see [MCP overview](#mcp-overview) for that workflow.

#### First run and API protection

Until the first administrator completes the setup wizard, SoAI refuses every request outside the wizard's own endpoints with `403` and `setup_required`, and that includes `/v1`. After setup, the compatible API stays open only while the API-key store holds no records, and creating the first record makes bearer authentication required for those requests.

**Revoking a key or letting it expire does not reopen the API, because the store counts every record rather than only the usable ones.** Select **Delete all keys** only when you intentionally want to remove every API-key record (including revoked or expired ones) and return the compatible API to the unauthenticated state. This does not grant or remove WebUI access.

While a key insert or deletion is in flight and its outcome is not yet known, SoAI treats protection as indeterminate and fails closed, so `/v1` returns `503` until the transaction settles and the store recounts. The security hardening audit reports the same state, so a `503` that persists points at the API-key registry rather than at a model or a plugin.

#### Create and manage a key in the SoAI WebUI

An administrator whose ACL grants **API key management** ([`OPENAI_API_ADMIN`](#acl-OPENAI_API_ADMIN)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then selects **Settings** from its menu. Open **[OpenAI](https://openai.com/)**. Under **[OpenAI](https://openai.com/) server API keys**, select **Create key**, enter a **Label (optional)**, and choose an **Expiration**. Copy the secret from the **API key created** dialog before closing it, because SoAI does not show the full value again, so store it in the client secret store rather than a project file. Every key begins with `soai-`, and the list keeps its first 12 characters so you can tell which key a client uses without holding the secret.

For example:

```
soai-AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODxAREhMUFRYXGBkaGxwdHh8
```

**Expiration** offers **90 days** or **Never**, and **Never** records no explicit expiry rather than making the key permanent. A key created without one inherits the instance default from [`API.OPENAI.SECURITY.KEY_EXPIRATION.DEFAULT_TTL_DAYS`](#config-API.OPENAI.SECURITY.KEY_EXPIRATION.DEFAULT_TTL_DAYS), which ships as 90 days, so a key that must not expire needs that setting changed to 0 first. [`API.OPENAI.SECURITY.KEY_EXPIRATION.ROTATION_REMINDER_DAYS`](#config-API.OPENAI.SECURITY.KEY_EXPIRATION.ROTATION_REMINDER_DAYS) ships as 75 days and drives the **Rotation due** marker in the list, which is a reminder and does not stop the key from authenticating.

In **Active keys**, use **Rotate** to issue a replacement and revoke the current key. The replacement keeps the original label and scope and shows its new secret once, and it takes the default expiration because rotation offers no expiration choice. A key that is already revoked cannot be rotated, so create a new one instead. **Revoke** stops a key from authenticating requests, while **Delete** permanently removes its record. Enable **Show revoked keys** when you need to audit or clean up old entries. **SoAI stores a salted HMAC-derived value and fingerprint, not a reusable plaintext copy.**

#### Set a key quota

Select **Limits** for a key. Choose **Unlimited**, **Tokens**, or **Requests**, then set one or more hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly limits. An hourly limit also needs its **Window (hours)**, a rolling window that [`API.OPENAI.KEY_QUOTAS.MAX_HOURLY_WINDOW_HOURS`](#config-API.OPENAI.KEY_QUOTAS.MAX_HOURLY_WINDOW_HOURS) caps at 720 hours. **Assigned user** appears for administrators. Assigning a user applies the key's quota to that user's WebUI chats and attributes requests made with the key to that account without changing what the key may do, and deleting the assigned account leaves the key unable to authenticate. **Saving quota settings resets usage tracking for that key.**

Quotas cap one key's requests or tokens over a usage window. They are separate from the instance-wide request limiter, which controls request frequency by remote client address. See [Rate limits and quotas](#rate-limits) for the difference and the default state.

#### What an API key permits

An SoAI API key carries only **Public inference API access** ([`OPENAI_API`](#acl-OPENAI_API)), and SoAI rejects any other scope when a key is created or rotated. **It does not give its holder a WebUI session, administrative access, shell access, or MCP access.** Configure the client with the exact authentication header and base URL shown in the [HTTP API reference](#http-api-reference). Keep the API on the private deployment boundary described in [Security hardening](#security-hardening), and configure its transport with [Network and TLS](#network-and-tls).

### Passwords and credential tools [page: passwords-and-credential-tools]

**SoAI handles several things that people casually call passwords, but they do not share one storage or trust model.** A WebUI login password, a saved website credential, an API key, and a string produced by `random_generate` pass through different code paths. Use the path designed for the secret you have.

#### What SoAI does with each credential

| Credential | How SoAI handles it | What matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WebUI account password | SoAI stores an [Argon2](https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2) hash and verifies the submitted password against it. The original password cannot be recovered from the database. | Use a separate password manager to store this password. The SoAI vault is available only after you sign in, so it cannot recover the password that unlocks the same account. |
| Saved website credential | SoAI encrypts the username and password with the installation encryption key and binds the entry to its owner and website origin. | SoAI must be able to decrypt this value for autofill. A person who obtains both the database and the encryption key can do the same. |
| API key, MCP token, or linked-account secret | Each subsystem has its own creation, storage, expiration, and revocation rules. | Do not treat these as WebUI passwords or save them in a conversation. Follow [Authentication and API keys](#authentication-and-api-keys) and the documentation for the owning integration. |
| `random_generate` output | The tool uses the operating system's cryptographic random source, including when `charset` is `password`, then returns the generated string as a normal tool result. | The model sees that result. A remote model provider may see it too. This is not the protected vault path. |

#### Choose a strong SoAI account password

SoAI accepts WebUI passwords from 8 to 1,024 characters. **Eight characters is the validation floor, not a security recommendation.** SoAI does not currently enforce its internal strength scorer, check a password against a breached-password list, or add a second authentication factor to WebUI login.

- Use a unique password for SoAI. Never reuse one from email, a model provider, an operating-system account, or another service.
- Prefer a password-manager-generated value of at least 15 characters. A longer passphrase made from unrelated words is a reasonable alternative when you must type it yourself.
- Length and uniqueness matter more than predictable substitutions or a forced mix of character classes.
- Keep the password in a reputable password manager protected by a strong, unique master password and multifactor authentication.
- Do not paste the password into Chat, a prompt, an automation, a project file, a shell command, or a support request.
- Change it after known or suspected disclosure, reuse on a compromised service, or unauthorized account activity. Routine changes without evidence of compromise usually encourage weaker, predictable passwords.

Login throttling slows online guessing but does not make a weak password safe. The default WebUI guard uses a five-minute window and a maximum of ten failures across client-address and account-related buckets. Keep SoAI behind the private deployment boundary described in [Security hardening](#security-hardening). If remote access needs a second factor, require it at the VPN or access gateway and make sure clients cannot bypass that boundary to reach SoAI directly.

#### How the protected credential path works

The protected path consists of five vault tools and two browser autofill tools. **These tools do not place the plaintext in their arguments or results.** The detailed controls and arguments are in [Secrets vault](#secrets-vault); the security flow is:

1. `vault_login_request` or `vault_secret_request` opens a credential form for the signed-in user.
2. The user enters the secret in that form, not in the conversation. SoAI returns an opaque handle and optional saved-entry metadata to the model.
3. The task handoff is encrypted and expires after ten minutes. Once claimed, the credential is held behind an in-memory handle bound to the user and conversation.
4. If the user saves it, SoAI encrypts the credential in the database and records its owner and website origin.
5. `browser_autofill_secret` or `browser_autofill_vault` checks the live browser origin, resolves the secret on the server, and fills the page without placing the plaintext in tool arguments or results.

`vault_list` and `vault_search` return labels, credential identifiers, origin scopes, dates, and a masked username hint. They do not return passwords. `vault_delete` removes one saved credential. Resetting **Password manager** deletes every saved credential owned by the signed-in user and invalidates that user's active secret handles.

#### Where the protection ends

The request and autofill tools do not return plaintext to the model. That is useful, but it is not a guarantee that another enabled browser tool cannot retrieve the value after it has been placed in the page.

- Prompt injection can still persuade an agent to request or use a credential. Read the site and reason shown in the approval prompt. Reject an unexpected login, an unfamiliar domain, or a request that does not match the task.
- Origin binding compares the URL scheme, canonical hostname, and explicit port. It blocks use on another origin, but it cannot tell whether the intended site is compromised or whether you approved a convincing lookalike domain.
- After a successful login, the browser session carries the account's authority. Other enabled browser tools can read or act as that account until the session is cleared or expires.
- `browser_type` refuses password and one-time-code fields, but `browser_eval` can run arbitrary JavaScript in the page. While a filled password remains in the DOM, an evaluation can read it and return it to the model. JavaScript evaluation is enabled by default and is not individually marked for approval.
- Origin binding controls where SoAI fills a credential. It does not control what scripts already running on that page do with the field value. The destination receives the password, and a compromised destination or injected page script can steal it.
- Vault encryption protects database contents without the installation key. It does not protect against an attacker who controls the SoAI process, the host account, the browser profile, or both the database and encryption key.
- Saved entries are isolated by SoAI user ID, but every credential tool still sits behind broad **MCP usage** ( [`MCP_USE`](#acl-MCP_USE) ). There is no separate vault ACL action.
- `vault_login_request`, both autofill tools, and `vault_delete` are individually marked for approval in Chat. `vault_secret_request` still requires the user to complete its credential form. `vault_list` and `vault_search` are not individually marked for approval and return their metadata without an approval prompt.
- Enabling **Allow plaintext secret replies** for a messaging account bypasses the protected Chat form. The messaging provider may retain the reply in history, notifications, logs, or backups.

#### Harden credential-tool access

- Leave vault and autofill tools out of a conversation or automation that does not need them. They are included in the default Execute-mode and automation tool sets, so review those selections before processing untrusted content.
- When a browser session will receive credentials, set [`TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.BROWSER.JS_EVAL_ENABLED) to `false` and leave `browser_eval` out of the selected tools. This removes the direct path for model-written JavaScript to read a filled password field.
- Keep per-call approval for autofill. A remembered approval is wider than one deliberate login and is a poor fit for high-value accounts.
- Do not add credential tools to [`TOOLS.MCP.SERVER_MODE.EXPOSED_TOOLS`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.SERVER_MODE.EXPOSED_TOOLS). They are absent from the default MCP server exposure list, and the security hardening audit flags them when added.
- Keep shell access disabled for agents that do not need it. A process with access to the SoAI data directory may reach the database and encryption key outside the vault-tool boundary.
- Protect backups and the installation encryption key separately. A database backup without the key cannot restore saved credentials; a copy containing both can expose them.
- Remove credentials that are no longer needed. Deletion has no undo, and changing a password at the destination does not remove the stale vault entry automatically.

#### If a password may be exposed

1. Change the password at the system that accepts it. Deleting a vault entry does not revoke the credential at that system.
2. Revoke that system's active sessions and tokens when it provides those controls.
3. Delete the old SoAI vault entry and clear any affected browser session before saving or using the replacement.
4. If the SoAI WebUI password is affected, change it and review active devices. SoAI revokes the account's earlier sessions when the password changes.
5. If the SoAI host, database, and encryption key may all have been exposed, rotate every credential stored in the vault, not only the one involved in the visible incident.
