### Network and TLS [page: network-and-tls]

SoAI exposes one main HTTP API and a small discovery service used by the WebUI to find the API. The default main port is `5090`. Discovery tries ports `7950` through `7960` and reports the API port, URL scheme, and edition state. Both [`SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.HOST`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.HOST) and [`SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.DISCOVERY_HOST`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.DISCOVERY_HOST) default to `0.0.0.0`, which listens on all interfaces. Review those values and [`SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.PORT`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.NETWORK.PORT) before exposing the service. In the SoAI WebUI, an administrator with the **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) permission selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, chooses **Settings**, selects **Advanced** in the page header, opens **Server**, changes the fields in the **Network** group, and selects **Save**.

#### HTTP and HTTPS

**TLS is off by default.** Enable it with [`SERVER.HTTP.SSL.TLS_ENABLED`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SSL.TLS_ENABLED). With user-supplied certificates, provide both [`SERVER.HTTP.SSL.CERT_FILE`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SSL.CERT_FILE) and [`SERVER.HTTP.SSL.KEY_FILE`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SSL.KEY_FILE); SoAI rejects an incomplete pair. SoAI creates a local self-signed certificate only when TLS is enabled and both fields are empty. Browsers and clients must trust that certificate or use a certificate issued for the deployment name.

SoAI requires TLS 1.2 or newer for the local TLS context and disables TLS compression. With a user-supplied server certificate and key, a configured CA file also makes SoAI require a client certificate trusted by that CA. It does not make SoAI's server certificate trusted by clients. Use [`SERVER.HTTP.SSL.CA_FILE`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SSL.CA_FILE) and [`SERVER.HTTP.SSL.KEY_PASSWORD`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SSL.KEY_PASSWORD) only with a complete certificate and key configuration.

#### Transport policy, proxies, and CORS

[`SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.REQUIRE_SECURE_TRANSPORT) rejects insecure requests, while [`SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT) redirects them only when local TLS is enabled or trusted proxy headers are active. HSTS is controlled by [`SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.ENFORCE_HSTS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.SECURITY.ENFORCE_HSTS). SoAI sends HSTS only on HTTPS responses. Test redirects and certificate trust before enabling HSTS for a hostname you cannot quickly recover.

If a TLS reverse proxy fronts SoAI, preserve the WebUI WebSocket upgrade and configure both [`SERVER.HTTP.PROXY.ENABLE_HEADERS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.PROXY.ENABLE_HEADERS) and [`SERVER.HTTP.PROXY.TRUSTED_NETWORKS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.PROXY.TRUSTED_NETWORKS). **Proxy headers are inactive until header support is enabled and at least one trusted network is listed.** Do not trust forwarded headers from arbitrary clients.

CORS is controlled by [`SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOWED_ORIGINS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOWED_ORIGINS) and [`SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOW_CREDENTIALS`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.CORS.ALLOW_CREDENTIALS). An empty allow-list does not enable cross-origin browser requests. If you add a wildcard or broad origin policy, replace it with the exact browser origins you use before exposing the service to other networks.

#### Binding and reverse proxies

Keep the discovery service on a trusted network and protect the main API with TLS, authentication, and a private network boundary. **A reverse proxy does not make public internet exposure a recommended deployment.** Prefer a VPN, such as [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com/) or a comparable private-network service, for remote access. See [Security hardening](#security-hardening) for the deployment policy and audit limits. For an additional application-level policy, review [`SERVER.HTTP.ACCESS_CONTROL.IP_WHITELIST`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.ACCESS_CONTROL.IP_WHITELIST) and [`SERVER.HTTP.ACCESS_CONTROL.IP_BLACKLIST`](#config-SERVER.HTTP.ACCESS_CONTROL.IP_BLACKLIST).

#### Public origin for messaging

[Telegram](https://telegram.org/) and [WhatsApp](https://www.whatsapp.com/) callbacks require a provider-reachable public HTTPS origin. [Discord](https://discord.com/) uses an outbound Gateway connection and does not require a public endpoint. Agent questions, tool approvals, and secure secret links require an HTTPS origin for all three providers, but a Discord-only origin can remain private if the messaging account owner can reach it. An administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)) selects the **Settings** button at the right of the header, chooses **Settings**, selects **Advanced**, opens **Server**, sets **Public origin**, and selects **Save**. The setting is [`SERVER.PUBLIC_ORIGIN`](#config-SERVER.PUBLIC_ORIGIN).

Enter the HTTPS base address without a provider callback path. SoAI builds the callback and authenticated Chat links from it. Publish `/api/v1/messaging/telegram/webhook` for [Telegram](https://telegram.org/) and `/api/v1/messaging/whatsapp/webhook` for [WhatsApp](https://www.whatsapp.com/), preserving the query string that SoAI adds. The WebUI, WebSocket, and other API routes do not need to be public for provider message delivery. If the account owner will open secure Chat links remotely, give that owner private access through a VPN or equivalent network boundary. See [Connect messaging apps to SoAI](#connect-messaging-apps-to-soai) for provider setup.

**Exposing SoAI directly to the public internet is not recommended.** Restrict public routing to the callback routes and keep the remaining interface behind a firewall or VPN. Read [Security hardening](#security-hardening) before configuring a public callback.

### Privacy and data handling [page: privacy-and-data-handling]

SoAI is self-hosted. Prompts, model inputs and outputs, conversations, documents, knowledge collections, files, credentials, API keys, logs, and hardware statistics stay on the host unless you choose a feature or provider that sends them elsewhere. **SoAI has no telemetry, usage analytics, crash reporting, heartbeat, background license check, remote support tunnel, or vendor administration channel.**

#### Network and offline boundaries

Local inference keeps request content on infrastructure you control. **A remote inference provider receives the input you send to it.** The same rule applies to configured search, image, mail, calendar, messaging, model-registry, and browser targets. Review each provider's terms and data handling before enabling it.

SoAI contacts [soai.to](https://soai.to/) for explicit licensing operations and update discovery and downloads. For release checks, it follows a redirect to the [GitHub](https://github.com/) API. Free Personal Use of SoAI Core needs no account, product key, or activation. These contacts do not include prompts, files, model output, credentials, or usage statistics.

##### Prepare for offline use

[Offline installation and operation](#offline-installation-and-operation) explains how to install runtime artifacts, backends, and models before blocking public-network access. Once [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE) is enabled, loopback and private-network services remain available while public provider calls, downloads, updates, web requests, and remote synchronization fail with an explicit error.

##### Runtime downloads

An installation path may obtain the managed [Python](https://www.python.org/) environment. First start can then fetch [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) [Chromium](https://www.chromium.org/), the managed Java runtime, Apache Tika, the ripgrep file-search binary, and tokenizer data. Browser automation can fetch [EasyList](https://easylist.to/) when ad blocking is enabled, and the network benchmark downloads a public test file only when you run it. Installing a backend or model contacts that backend's package and model sources. **These are downloads to the SoAI host; SoAI does not attach prompt or usage data to them.** The current host list and exact conditions are in `PRIVACY.md` at the root of the [SoAI repository](https://github.com/GetSoAI/SoAI).

#### Retention and incident response

The operator controls filesystem access, encryption at rest, backups, retention, and deletion. Use [Data storage, retention, and relocation](#data-storage-retention-and-relocation) to locate each data class, then use the owning WebUI workflow for ordinary deletion. If you operate SoAI for other people, you are responsible for the lawful basis, access policy, retention schedule, and data-subject requests for their data.

##### Report an unexpected connection

**Treat an undisclosed outbound connection as a security defect.** Follow [Security updates and vulnerability reporting](#security-updates-and-vulnerability-reporting) and do not include credentials or private user data in the report. The separate website privacy notice, available from **Privacy** in the [soai.to](https://soai.to/) footer, governs licensing-site, checkout, and direct support records; it does not describe the self-hosted application data above.

### Security updates and vulnerability reporting [page: security-updates-and-vulnerability-reporting]

SoAI receives security support from **22 August 2026 through 22 August 2031**. Security fixes are delivered through the same signed, numbered release path as other SoAI updates and are free of charge, regardless of whether an installation is personal, evaluation, or commercial.

The supported baseline is the latest available stable SoAI release. **To remain supported, update to that release; superseded releases are not maintained for feature parity or guaranteed separate security fixes.**

#### Check updates and read advisories

1. In the SoAI WebUI, open the **Settings** menu at the right of the header, then **Updates**. This requires **Software updates** ( [`SOFTWARE_UPDATE`](#acl-SOFTWARE_UPDATE) ).
2. Select **Check for updates**.
3. Review the current version, available version, release notes, and platform support shown on the page.
4. On a supported [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/), [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/), or [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) installation, select **Install update** and confirm the dialog.
5. Wait for the updating screen to reconnect after SoAI restarts.

The updater authenticates the signed release manifest and verifies the selected artifact before installation. It keeps the last valid installation when verification or installation fails. **Update checks require public-network access and are unavailable while [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE) is enabled.** [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) and [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) use manifest-authenticated complete archives, while [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) uses the current manifest-authenticated x64 installer record. See [Updating SoAI](#updating-soai) for platform-specific installation, backup, and recovery steps.

##### Read advisories

Open the [SoAI repository](https://github.com/GetSoAI/SoAI), then select **Security > Advisories** for public advisories. They are also referenced by [Release notes and upgrade notices](#release-notes-and-upgrade-notices). The support period and software bill of materials are recorded in `SECURITY.md` at the repository root.

#### Report vulnerabilities and understand response targets

Email [security@soai.to](mailto:security@soai.to) with the subject **SoAI security report**. Include the affected version or revision, platform, prerequisite access, reproduction steps, impact, and a safe proof of concept. Do not send live credentials, private user data, or a destructive payload. Ask for a secure transfer method before sending sensitive attachments.

**Do not open a public issue with exploit details or publish an undisclosed vulnerability.** Test only systems and data you own or are explicitly authorized to test. The policy excludes denial-of-service testing, persistence, social engineering, data exfiltration, and testing against other users.

##### Response targets

| Stage | Target |
| --- | --- |
| Acknowledge receipt | 5 business days |
| Initial assessment and severity decision | 10 business days |
| Fix or documented mitigation for a confirmed high or critical issue | 90 days |
| Public advisory | When the fix ships, or 90 days after acknowledgement, whichever comes first |

These are coordinated-disclosure targets, not a paid support service level. An actively exploited issue is treated as critical. Reporter credit is available on request.

### Download and verify SoAI releases [page: download-and-verify-soai-releases]

Open the official [SoAI repository](https://github.com/GetSoAI/SoAI), select **Releases**, and download the required Core files. A numbered Core release set includes its platform artifacts, exact SHA-256 sidecars, the primary V1 JSON release manifest, the separately signed [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) and Windows-archive V1 manifests, their Ed25519 signatures, and an upload inventory. **The source ZIP and TAR files that [GitHub](https://github.com/) generates are source snapshots, not runnable products or update payloads.**

#### Choose the product artifact

| Platform | Artifact | Update path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) x64 or arm64 | `SoAI-<version>-linux-complete.zip` | Manifest-authenticated complete archive |
| [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) x64 | `SoAI-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe` or `SoAI-<version>-windows-x64-complete.zip` | Manifest-authenticated installer for updates; separately authenticated complete archive with compiled launcher |
| [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) [Intel](https://www.intel.com/) or [Apple](https://www.apple.com/) silicon | `SoAI-<version>-macos-complete.zip` | Manifest-authenticated complete archive |

SoAI Connect has a separate repository, version, signing identity, and release path. **Its APK and checksum are not part of the SoAI Core signed manifest.** See [Install SoAI Core](#install-soai-core) for the supported installation path on each platform.

SoAI OS is not yet available and is not currently distributed, so no appliance release set is published. An appliance release set uses the `SoAI-OS-<version>-linux-complete.zip` archive, and its manifest and inventory use the same `SoAI-OS-<version>` prefix, so Core and appliance files never share one verification directory. Contact [info@soai.to](mailto:info@soai.to) to join the waitlist; joining does not grant a license or promise an availability date.

#### Verify authenticity and integrity

**A matching checksum detects accidental or malicious file changes only if the checksum itself is trusted.** The signed manifests authenticate the release artifacts and bind artifact names, platforms, sizes, hashes, archive roots, and every regular file in each complete archive. The separately signed Windows-archive V1 manifest authenticates the [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) complete ZIP without changing the exact primary V1 automatic-update manifest shape. Compare the production public-key fingerprint with a trusted source copy:

```
e0333589b1ca792397182cc3f843989c021a056c61e281f8456c1da4f479f2a7
```

#### Run the offline verifier

From a trusted existing installation or complete source tree with its managed runtime installed, place the exact release set in one directory. Run the verifier from the installation or source-tree root with the edition, release version, Core version, pinned public key, and expected fingerprint:

##### Linux and macOS

```
PYTHONPATH=backend soai_main_venv/bin/python -m app.updater.offline_release_verification \
  --artifacts-directory /path/to/release-files \
  --version <version> \
  --core-version <core-version> \
  --edition soai-core \
  --public-key backend/app/updater/release_public_key.txt \
  --expected-public-key-sha256 e0333589b1ca792397182cc3f843989c021a056c61e281f8456c1da4f479f2a7
```

##### Windows PowerShell

```
$env:PYTHONPATH = "backend"
.\soai_main_venv\Scripts\python.exe -m app.updater.offline_release_verification `
  --artifacts-directory C:\path\to\release-files `
  --version <version> `
  --core-version <core-version> `
  --edition soai-core `
  --public-key backend\app\updater\release_public_key.txt `
  --expected-public-key-sha256 e0333589b1ca792397182cc3f843989c021a056c61e281f8456c1da4f479f2a7
```

The verifier accepts `--edition soai-os` for an appliance release set, with the SoAI OS and Core version values that belong to that release.

The verifier fails closed if an expected file is missing or extra, the key fingerprint differs, the signature is invalid, an artifact or sidecar differs, a platform payload is incomplete, or an archive inventory does not match. **Proceed only after it prints that the signature, checksums, artifacts, and archive inventories are valid.**

#### Use the in-application updater

With **Software updates** ([`SOFTWARE_UPDATE`](#acl-SOFTWARE_UPDATE)), open the **Settings** menu at the right of the header in the SoAI WebUI, then **Updates**. On supported [Linux](https://www.kernel.org/) and [macOS](https://www.apple.com/macos/) installations, SoAI verifies the matching signed manifest and selected archive before applying it. [Windows](https://www.microsoft.com/windows/) verifies the primary manifest and hands off the current x64 installer. See [Updating SoAI](#updating-soai) for the complete backup, installation, and recovery workflow.

### Licensing administration [page: licensing-administration]

The Licensing page in the SoAI WebUI reports the declaration and entitlement that the running installation is enforcing, and it is an operational view rather than a substitute for the accepted license or entitlement certificate. Read [License and legal](#license-and-legal) before making a licensing decision.

#### Open Licensing and read the summary

Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, choose **Settings**, then open the **Licensing** tab, which is available only to an Administrator with **Licensing administration** ([`LICENSING_ADMIN`](#acl-LICENSING_ADMIN)).

**Deployment license** shows the current status, the edition and version, when the license was accepted and the fingerprint of the accepted document, when the current declaration took effect, and the declaration itself with any verified entitlement beside it. A deployment holding an entitlement also shows its environment, licensed capabilities, and deployment allowances, together with the included support hours when the entitlement records them. A fixed-term or continuity entitlement adds its effective time and term boundaries, while a perpetual entitlement shows no term rows because it has none.

A **Restart SoAI** item with an **Open Power** control appears when licensing is ready but the process started with limited services, which happens after a recovery that succeeded on a process that had started in a restricted state. SoAI records that restart requirement itself, so the notification stays until the process restarts.

#### When licensing restricts the instance

Several recorded states hold the instance in a repair plane: an expired evaluation or commercial term, a suspended or terminated entitlement, an entitlement whose signature, binding, or contract does not validate, a system clock that has moved more than 5 minutes behind the last verified time, and a deployment that has accepted the license but has no usable declaration or entitlement yet. In that condition SoAI answers ordinary requests with `403` and `licensing_restricted`, so inference, chat, model and plugin administration, configuration changes, updates, the terminal, and the compatible API all refuse work.

What stays available is what recovery needs: signing in, notifications, cancelling a request, Power, Backup, reading models, plugins, hardware, logs, and system status, reading Files, and the Licensing page itself. **Recovering the instance means correcting the licensing state rather than restarting into it.** An entitlement within 7 days of its term end reports an expiring status, which warns without restricting anything.

#### Declare how the deployment is used

During Core setup, the wizard shows the controlling license with its fingerprint, then asks how the deployment will be used. **Personal use** is the only choice you can select, and **Organization or commercial use** stays visible but disabled because commercial licenses and organization evaluations are not currently being issued. Choose **Personal use** only when the deployment satisfies the personal-use terms shown in the wizard, then confirm the attestation, and if the disabled choice describes the deployment, do not declare Personal Use to get past the step. Contact [info@soai.to](mailto:info@soai.to) for licensing information.

SoAI Core under a Personal Use declaration needs no entitlement, while SoAI OS and any organization declaration require one, so the page follows the recorded state and a delivered entitlement shows different controls from a new Personal Use installation. **Change license type** moves the declaration afterwards, and the direction back to Personal Use retires the active entitlement, which is also why the organization direction stays disabled on a personal deployment.

#### Manage an entitlement

- **License** and **Accept license** appear while the current license document has not been accepted, and acceptance records the exact version and fingerprint shown.
- **Activate license** appears once the license is accepted on a deployment that needs an entitlement and has none. The button stays disabled until you enter a key of at least 16 characters, accepting the governing documents is part of the action, and an organization declaration also asks for the deployment environment.
- **Convert to commercial**, **Convert to organization OS evaluation**, **Revert OS evaluation to personal use**, **Change deployment environment**, and **Retrieve renewed term** appear only under an organization or commercial declaration whose entitlement supports online maintenance, and each one also depends on the current entitlement type and product.
- A deployment activated from an offline certificate has no online maintenance, so those controls and **Deactivate deployment** do not appear for it.

**A disabled control is not permission to bypass the WebUI restriction.**

##### Recover or move an entitlement

**Reconcile activation** appears when the last operation's outcome is unknown, which is the case when its response was lost rather than refused. SoAI already retries such an operation in the background on a widening delay and cancels a merely prepared operation at the next start, so use the control when you want that attempt made now.

**Export offline request** and **Import offline certificate** appear once the license is accepted on a deployment that requires an entitlement and no other licensing operation is running. Export downloads `soai-offline-activation-request-v1.json`, and Import accepts the returned `.soailicense` certificate. **Keep both files with the deployment they were created for, because the certificate is bound to that deployment's identity.**

**Deactivate deployment** appears only when the entitlement supports online maintenance. Choose **Rehost**, **Retired**, **Disaster recovery**, or **Other** as the fixed reason. Deactivation releases the authority binding and replaces the local deployment identity, so reactivation or recovery is required before that entitlement can be used again; back up required data first and do not repeat a request whose outcome is still being reconciled. Licensing attempts are limited per client address, and 6 online operations in 600 seconds is the point where SoAI answers with `429` instead of contacting the licensing service, so read the error on a failed attempt rather than retrying in a loop.

The licensing state lives in the primary database, and the deployment's private key is stored encrypted with the installation encryption key. Both are default backup targets, and restore validates them as a pair, refusing a backup that carries one without the other or that was written by the other edition. Keep both targets enabled if you want a backup you can recover an entitlement from, as described in [Backup](#backup).

#### Privacy and outage behavior

A licensing request carries the instance identifier, the deployment identity and its public key, a random nonce, the SoAI version, and the fields the selected action needs, such as the product key, the deployment environment, or the identifier, version, fingerprint, and acceptance time of each governing document. Each request is signed with the key pair created for this deployment and goes only to [soai.to](https://soai.to/). **Requests do not include prompts, model content, files, credentials, hardware fingerprints, or usage statistics.** The identifiers and acceptance records that a request does send are used only to issue and maintain that entitlement, and they are never sold, shared with an advertiser, mined, or used to train a model.

Entitlement validation is local after activation and SoAI runs no licensing heartbeat, so a licensing-service outage does not by itself invalidate a valid local entitlement, and the background recovery worker contacts the service only while an operation is still unresolved. With [`SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE`](#config-SYSTEM.RUNTIME.STAY_OFFLINE) enabled, online licensing actions fail like other public calls, so use the offline export and import path instead. See [Privacy and data handling](#privacy-and-data-handling) for the complete boundary.

## Performance

### Make the WebUI faster on low-end clients [page: make-the-webui-faster-on-low-end-clients]

Client tuning cuts browser work on the computer where the SoAI WebUI is open, and it changes presentation only, so model speed, queue depth, and server capacity are unaffected. Use [Make SoAI faster on low-end servers](#make-soai-faster-on-low-end-servers) for the SoAI host and [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) for inference limits.

Most of what follows lives in one place. In the WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then **Settings**. The **General** and **Theme** tabs are open to every signed-in account and both commit from the page-header **Save**, while a few controls carry their own **Edit** and **Save** instead.

#### Cut motion and compositing

**Settings > Theme > Motion** holds the three settings with the largest effect on a slow client.

1. Turn **Disable animations** on.
2. Turn **Auto-hide page header** off.
3. Turn **Glass effects** off.
4. Select the page-header **Save**.

**Disable animations** sets every transition and animation duration in the WebUI to 0, which also makes the **Page transitions**, **Modal animation**, **Notification animation**, and **Animation speed** controls below it inert. If your operating system already has its reduce-motion setting on, the WebUI honors that and those durations are already 0 before you change anything. Where you would rather keep the motion, setting **Animation speed** to **Fast** shortens it instead of removing it.

**Glass effects** is off by default, so this is usually a check rather than a change. Turning it on applies backdrop blur to modals, menus, the sidebar, the header, and chat surfaces, and blur is the most expensive presentation option in the WebUI. [Firefox](https://www.mozilla.org/firefox/) and Firefox-based browsers tend to show the cost first, usually as stutter while scrolling and more so when hardware acceleration is unavailable.

**Auto-hide page header** folds and extends the header as you scroll, so turning it off keeps the header at a fixed height and removes that work. It has no effect on a small display, where the header does not fold at all.

#### Reduce what the page draws

##### Background

A wallpaper puts a full-window image and a darkness overlay behind the whole interface, and it is shared by every account rather than being yours alone. On a low-end client, use the default background or a solid color.

1. Open **Settings > Theme > Background**.
2. If a wallpaper is set, the first row reads **Remove custom wallpaper**. Select **Remove**.
3. To use a color instead, set **Solid background color**, then select the page-header **Save**.

**The color control is inactive while a wallpaper exists, which is why the order matters.** What appears under **Background** depends on your permissions: an Administrator with **UI customization** ([`WEBUI_APPEARANCE_ADMIN`](#acl-WEBUI_APPEARANCE_ADMIN)) gets upload, download, overlay, information, and removal, an Administrator without it sees only **Solid background color**, and any other account sees no **Background** group and needs an administrator to remove a shared wallpaper. [Personal preferences](#personal-preferences) covers wallpaper administration in full.

##### Chat rendering

Two settings decide what a long conversation costs to display. **Settings > Theme > Code blocks > Code recognition** detects a block's programming language and marks up its syntax tokens, and turning it off leaves ordinary blocks as plain text while diff blocks and [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/) diagrams still render. Reach for it first when chats full of large code blocks are slow.

**Render rich text (Markdown)** goes considerably further and lives with the conversation rather than in Settings, under **Chat configuration** on the **Appearance** tab. With it off, each message body becomes one escaped paragraph, so the browser skips Markdown parsing, tables, code block rendering, and inline preview tokens together. That supersedes **Code recognition** and costs you every rendered element in the transcript, so treat it as the option for a client that cannot keep up rather than a default. **Inline multimedia previews** sits beside it and stops the WebUI from resolving and embedding previews for media links and path references, which is per-message work that runs after the message is drawn.

##### Dashboard sections

1. Open **Settings > Theme > Dashboard**.
2. Find **Dashboard elements** and select **Edit**.
3. Turn off the sections you do not read, then select **Save** in **Dashboard elements**.

The editor lists what the current edition offers, which can include clock, logs, requests, throughput, network, plugins, models, hardware widgets, image, memo, and quick actions. **System status** is required and its toggle stays locked on. A hidden section is never created, so it costs no DOM, no redraws, and none of its own updates, though hiding it does not stop server-side collection or release every shared Dashboard subscription. Use [Make SoAI faster on low-end servers](#make-soai-faster-on-low-end-servers) when the collection itself should stop.

##### List view for large collections

**Models**, **Plugins**, and **Prompts** offer card and list views, and **Files** offers icon and list views. On each page, select the view control in the page header until its label reads **List view**; below roughly 1024 px of width, or whenever the actions no longer fit, they collapse behind **More actions** in the page header. List view swaps card and icon surfaces for compact rows, which cuts layout and paint work on a long collection while requesting the same records. **Each page remembers its own choice in the current browser rather than in your account, so it does not follow you to another machine.**

Models needs **Model read access** ([`MODEL_READ`](#acl-MODEL_READ)), Plugins needs **Plugin read access** ([`PLUGIN_READ`](#acl-PLUGIN_READ)), and Files needs **Files reading** ([`FILE_EXPLORER_READ`](#acl-FILE_EXPLORER_READ)), and without the page's access neither the page nor its view control appears. Prompts needs only a signed-in account.

#### Reduce timers and live updates

1. Open **Settings > General** and find **Behavior**.
2. Turn **Show seconds** off, which drops the clock from once per second to once per minute.
3. Turn **Header clock** off if you do not need it, which stops its timer entirely and takes the seconds display with it.
4. Turn **Live status overlay** off if you do not use it.
5. Select **Save**.

Both **Show seconds** and **Live status overlay** are off by default, so these are worth confirming before you go looking elsewhere. The overlay subscribes to connection, latency, queue, and event telemetry and refreshes its diagnostics every 15 seconds, and turning it off removes the overlay, its listeners, and that timer without disabling server monitoring.

Dashboard, Hardware, Metrics, and Logs keep processing their updates the whole time you are viewing them, so navigate away when you finish monitoring and the router releases that page's renderers, timers, and subscriptions. If Logs has to stay open, choose **100 lines** rather than the default of 250, or 500, 1000, 2000, or 5000, to keep its rendered log DOM small. Dashboard needs **System status access** ([`SYSTEM_STATUS_READ`](#acl-SYSTEM_STATUS_READ)), Hardware needs **Hardware read access** ([`HARDWARE_READ`](#acl-HARDWARE_READ)), and Logs needs **Log access** ([`LOG_ACCESS`](#acl-LOG_ACCESS)), while Metrics appears for every signed-in account.

#### Avoid duplicate runtimes

Keep one SoAI browser tab open when you can, and close a detached Chat window once you are done with it. Every tab and every detached window starts its own frontend runtime, holds its own WebSocket connection, and runs whatever its active page needs, so closing an unused copy reclaims that client's timers, DOM, and live subscriptions without touching the signed-in session in the window you keep.

#### Check the result

1. Open the browser's task manager or your operating system's process monitor and note the tab's CPU and memory use.
2. Reload SoAI after saving the settings above.
3. Repeat the same scrolling, Dashboard, collection, and code-heavy chat actions.
4. Keep each change whose visual or informational tradeoff suits how you work.

**A slow response with a responsive interface is a server or model problem rather than this one.** Stutter while scrolling, animating, highlighting code, or updating widgets is the client-side case these settings address.

### Make SoAI faster on low-end servers [page: make-soai-faster-on-low-end-servers]

Server tuning cuts the work SoAI does on its own host: the background collection, indexing, synchronization, and maintenance that runs whether or not anyone is using the instance. It does not make a model generate faster and it does not raise how many requests the host can carry at once, so use [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) to size the workload and [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning) for admission, concurrency, and idle unloading.

#### Change a server setting

Every control on this page is a Core configuration path, and changing one requires an Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)).

1. In the SoAI WebUI, select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then **Settings**.
2. Select **Advanced** in the page header.
3. Paste the full configuration path into **Search settings...**, change the value, and select **Save**.
4. Select **Restart SoAI** when the WebUI reports a pending restart.

**Every setting on this page needs that restart, because SoAI reloads only routing, API rate limiting, and its runtime section in place.** Change one group at a time so a saving is attributable and a capability you no longer have is easy to trace back.

#### Stop unused plugin runtimes

An enabled local plugin can own a backend process and the model runtime inside it, which is usually the largest thing running beside inference. Open **Plugins**, turn the switch off for a plugin the instance does not serve requests from, and wait for the disable task to finish. Disabling purges that plugin's queued work, stops its active runtime, and moves it to a disabled state that blocks new work until you enable it again. The page requires **Plugin read access** ([`PLUGIN_READ`](#acl-PLUGIN_READ)) and the switch requires **Plugin administration** ([`PLUGIN_ADMIN`](#acl-PLUGIN_ADMIN)).

**Stop plugin** is a different action, since it ends the current runtime and leaves the plugin enabled, so the next request that routes to it starts it again. Use the switch for a backend that should not serve requests at all and **Stop plugin** when you only want the memory back now. Do not disable a plugin to limit how many backends run at once, because that is [`MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS) and belongs in [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning).

The plugin's own state can hold the switch. A quarantined, hardware-incompatible, permanently disabled, or override-pending plugin locks it and relabels it with the state name instead of **Enabled**, and a plugin with an operation in flight holds it until that operation settles. [Install and manage plugins](#install-and-manage-plugins) covers those states.

#### Reduce monitoring collection

##### Hardware

A sampling thread collects CPU, memory, storage, network, and GPU readings every 3 seconds by default, publishes each snapshot to live consumers, and writes samples to the database while history is on.

- [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.HARDWARE_HISTORY_ENABLED) set to `false` is the first thing to try, because it stops the database writes and the hourly retention pass while the live snapshot and its broadcast continue. Chart then shows **History is disabled by the backend.**
- [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.MONITORING_INTERVAL_MS) raised from `3000` samples less often, so `10000` turns 3 seconds into 10 and cuts the collection work with it.
- [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DETAILED_GPU_INFO`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.DETAILED_GPU_INFO) set to `false` drops the per-GPU running-process query, which is the data behind the Hardware process card, and leaves utilization, memory, drivers, and adapters intact.
- [`SYSTEM.HARDWARE.ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.HARDWARE.ENABLED) set to `false` stops the sampling thread and the minimum-specs check.

**Turning the service off is narrower than it sounds.** The Hardware page keeps answering, because its snapshot and capability endpoints query the host on demand rather than reading the sampling thread's output, so live readings survive. What actually stops is the periodic collection behind history and the live displays, along with the `hardware_snapshot` agent tool, GPU control, and SoAIBench, which each check the service and refuse while it is off. Disable history instead when the goal is only to stop database growth.

##### Metrics

Request accounting, stored history, and the live broadcast to the WebUI are three separate workloads, so you can reduce two of them and keep the counts.

- [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.ENABLED`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.ENABLED) set to `false` stops the periodic history samples, written every 3000 ms by default, and their retention pass. SoAI keeps counting requests and keeps flushing the current aggregate to the database every 30 seconds, so Metrics still works and only the charts and exports lose their history.
- [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.LOGGING_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.METRICS_HISTORY.LOGGING_INTERVAL_MS) raised keeps history at a coarser granularity.
- [`OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.BROADCAST_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.METRICS.BROADCAST_INTERVAL_MS) raised from `1000` publishes live snapshots less often, and Metrics and Dashboard values react more slowly. It saves nothing on an idle server, because the broadcast checks for a subscriber before it builds the snapshot, so no open WebUI already means no work.

Hardware history and metrics history are independent, and disabling one leaves the other running. [Monitoring and observability](#monitoring-and-observability) lists the retention settings and the full default set.

#### Turn off subsystems you do not use

[`TOOLS.RAG.ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.RAG.ENABLED) ships on, and while it is on SoAI initializes the RAG service, starts its processing workers, and spawns a [Chroma](https://www.trychroma.com/) worker process for each storage shard, which is real memory and process overhead on a host that never indexes a document. Set it to `false` on a server with no Knowledge collections, no document indexing, no RAG retrieval, and no RAG-backed web ingestion. Those capabilities stay unavailable until you enable it again and restart.

[`TOOLS.MCP.ENABLED`](#config-TOOLS.MCP.ENABLED) is the broader switch, because RAG starts from inside the MCP runtime rather than beside it, so turning MCP off stops the registered tool system and RAG together. **Use it only for an inference-only server, since Chat and automations lose every MCP-backed tool with it.**

#### Slow the recurring background tasks

##### Mail and calendar

Mail synchronization polls every 120 seconds by default and calendar synchronization every 300 seconds, and each pass reads the linked accounts, contacts the remote service for the ones that are due, and updates the cached data. Set [`INTEGRATIONS.MAIL.SYNC.ENABLED`](#config-INTEGRATIONS.MAIL.SYNC.ENABLED) or [`INTEGRATIONS.CALENDAR.SYNC.ENABLED`](#config-INTEGRATIONS.CALENDAR.SYNC.ENABLED) to `false` when the server has no linked accounts of that kind, or raise [`INTEGRATIONS.MAIL.SYNC.INTERVAL_SEC`](#config-INTEGRATIONS.MAIL.SYNC.INTERVAL_SEC) and [`INTEGRATIONS.CALENDAR.SYNC.INTERVAL_SEC`](#config-INTEGRATIONS.CALENDAR.SYNC.INTERVAL_SEC) when you want the sync but not that often, accepting that remote changes take longer to appear.

Calendar reminder delivery is separate and unaffected. It runs on its own 60 second task, reads reminders already stored in SoAI, and keeps firing whether or not calendar synchronization is on.

##### Model discovery

SoAI asks every installed plugin for model metadata on a timer that starts with the server and does not depend on a catalog page being open. Raise [`MODELS.MANAGER.PERFORMANCE.BACKGROUND_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS`](#config-MODELS.MANAGER.PERFORMANCE.BACKGROUND_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS) from its default of `60000` when the available models seldom change, and a model added outside SoAI then waits until the next refresh to appear.

##### Database maintenance and backups

At startup, SoAI checks whether the [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) database is due for VACUUM maintenance to reclaim unused disk space. The default interval is 720 hours (30 days) since the last successful run, and maintenance is skipped when there is too little space to reclaim. This avoids unnecessary disk work and can add time to startup when maintenance is needed. [`DATA.DATABASE.SQLITE.VACUUM_INTERVAL_HOURS`](#config-DATA.DATABASE.SQLITE.VACUUM_INTERVAL_HOURS) controls the interval; setting it to `0` disables automatic VACUUM, leaving unused space in the database file available for reuse.

A scheduled backup reads the selected targets, writes an archive, and applies retention, every 24 hours by default. **Interval hours** sits on the **Backup** tab, which an Administrator with **Backup administration** ([`BACKUP_ADMIN`](#acl-BACKUP_ADMIN)) can open, and [`DATA.BACKUP.SCHEDULE.INTERVAL_HOURS`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.SCHEDULE.INTERVAL_HOURS) is the same value in Advanced settings. Setting it to `0` stops the recurring schedule while **Create backup** stays available and [`DATA.BACKUP.ENABLED`](#config-DATA.BACKUP.ENABLED) remains `true`, and SoAI still takes the one backup it requires the first time a target has never completed one.

Keep backups. Change their timing only after measuring backup I/O against the active workload, and read [Backup](#backup) first.

#### Keep logging useful

Keep [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOG_LEVEL`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.LOG_LEVEL) at `INFO` or a higher severity during normal use. `DEBUG` and `TRACE`, the level below `DEBUG`, add formatting, buffering, and write work at every call site they enable, so use them for a bounded investigation and put the level back afterwards. If nothing consumes the process console output, [`OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.CONSOLE_LOGGING`](#config-OBSERVABILITY.LOGGING.CONSOLE_LOGGING) set to `false` removes the duplicate console write while the main log file and the WebUI log stream keep their own handlers.

Application logs are the evidence for diagnosing a backend or plugin failure, so leave the main log on.

#### Measure the result

1. Record idle CPU, memory, and disk activity on the host, with the database size, before you change anything.
2. Apply one change, restart, and let the services settle.
3. Repeat the same idle window and the same request workload.
4. Keep the change when the saving is worth the slower updates or the capability you gave up.

Measure from the operating system rather than from SoAI, because several of these settings change the very readings Hardware and Metrics report.

### Storage paths and host capacity [page: storage-paths-and-host-capacity]

Host capacity is the physical boundary for model files, plugin runtimes, database traffic, request queues, and local inference. Choose a storage location for each growing data class, leave recovery headroom, and measure the workload on the host that will run it. Use the guidance below for host resources and filesystem placement. For scheduler controls, use [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning).

#### Plan storage capacity

[`SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA`](#config-SYSTEM.PATHS.SYSTEM_DATA) is the root for most durable state. Models, managed plugin backends, plugin environments, files, the database, Knowledge indexes, logs, and backups have separate child paths and can be placed on different volumes. Installed `.soaiplugin` packages remain relative to the application base.

Use [Data storage, retention, and relocation](#data-storage-retention-and-relocation) for the complete ownership map and safe relocation sequence. **A configuration change does not move existing data.**

##### Place data by access pattern

| Data class | Capacity characteristic | Placement concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary database | Small relative to models, but latency-sensitive and continuously updated. | Use reliable local storage with correct ownership. Do not share one live database between instances. |
| Models and plugin runtimes | Usually the largest static or slowly changing data. | Prioritize capacity and read throughput. Keep enough temporary headroom for downloads, extraction, cloning, and updates. |
| Managed files and Knowledge indexes | Grows with user uploads and indexed content. | Plan both original files and derived index data; removing a collection is a data operation, not a filesystem shortcut. |
| Logs and metrics history | Continuous writes controlled by retention and sampling. | Keep diagnostic history long enough for operations, then tune collection only after measuring write pressure. |
| Backups | Can duplicate a large share of durable state. | Keep a verified copy off the host. Ensure source and destination have space for an in-progress backup. |

##### Keep disk admission headroom

SoAI reserves capacity before supported model and plugin downloads, uploads, backups, archive extraction, browser downloads, and Knowledge writes. Durable inference admission also checks [`MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT), which defaults to 268,435,456 bytes. A reserve rejection is a capacity signal, not a reason to bypass validation.

Monitor the exact filesystem that owns each configured path. **Free space on the installation volume does not help a model store or backup destination mounted elsewhere.** Account for filesystem overhead, temporary files, retained backups, database growth, and the old copy kept during a safe relocation.

#### Plan memory and compute capacity

**Model weights are only part of memory demand.** Context, key-value cache, backend workspace, batching, concurrent requests, plugin processes, Core, browser workers, and the operating system also consume RAM or VRAM. Measure the selected model, quantization, context size, and backend together. Do not infer capacity from parameter count or GPU memory alone.

A remote-provider model avoids local inference memory but still uses Core, network, queue, transcript, tool, and file-processing resources. A CPU backend shares system memory with the application and host. Leave enough headroom for failure handling and maintenance instead of planning around a peak that already causes swapping or allocation failures.

##### Separate compute bottlenecks

- GPU or CPU saturation during inference belongs to the selected model, backend, and concurrency.
- Slow model loading can be storage throughput, model size, backend initialization, or device allocation.
- A growing queue with idle hardware can indicate routing, provider, plugin, or per-owner limits.
- A responsive server with a stuttering page is client rendering; use [Personal preferences](#personal-preferences).

In the SoAI WebUI, use **Hardware** and **Metrics** together. Hardware shows device, memory, temperature, power, storage, and network state; Metrics shows request, latency, token, queue, plugin, and model activity. Retained values after a disconnect are not current until the WebSocket supplies a fresh snapshot.

#### Maintain and measure the host

Updates and path moves can temporarily require both old and new copies. Recovery requires a readable database, matching encryption key, owned file data, and a verified backup outside the failure domain. **A single large volume may be simple, but it is not an independent backup.** Before increasing workload, verify that the host can still create a backup and restart cleanly under the expected disk and memory pressure.

##### Measure one change at a time

1. Record free space, disk activity, memory, queue depth, model load time, and request latency.
2. Repeat a representative workload with known model, prompt length, concurrency, and tool use.
3. Change one placement or capacity variable.
4. Repeat the workload and keep the change only when the result and recovery margin improve.

### Scheduler and runtime tuning [page: scheduler-and-runtime-tuning]

Runtime tuning controls how SoAI admits work, how much of it runs at once, how long an attempt may take, and when idle model memory is released. This page holds those controls and their factory values, while [Resilience and self-healing](#resilience-and-self-healing) describes what the scheduler does with them under failure and [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) covers choosing values for a measured workload. Raising a limit moves pressure somewhere else, usually to memory, a provider quota, or a backend that was already saturated, so change one control at a time and read completed throughput rather than queue depth.

#### Change a routing setting in the SoAI WebUI

Opening Advanced settings requires an Administrator with **Configuration changes** ([`CONFIG_PATCH`](#acl-CONFIG_PATCH)).

1. Select the **Settings** button at the right of the header, then **Settings**.
2. Select **Advanced** in the page header.
3. Paste the full configuration path into **Search settings...**, change the value, and select **Save**.
4. Select **Restart SoAI** if the WebUI reports a pending restart.

[`MODELS.ROUTING`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING) is one of the three sections SoAI reloads in place, so a save under it usually applies at once: SoAI rebuilds the routing configuration and hands it to the queue, the scheduler, the executor, the capacity service, and the Plugin Guardian. The exceptions matter more than the rule.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_LIMITS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_LIMITS) and [`MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_TIMEOUTS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_TIMEOUTS) record a pending restart, because the shared HTTP client is built once at startup, and SoAI compares them against the values the process started with rather than against the previous save, so restoring them clears the pending restart they created. Lowering [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NUM_PLANNER_WORKERS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NUM_PLANNER_WORKERS) logs that it will apply on restart, while raising it spawns the extra workers immediately.

A second group is easier to miss, because those settings are read once while SoAI starts and never picked up by a reload, and since they live under a reloadable section the WebUI reports nothing. Restart the process yourself after changing [`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS), [`MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT), [`MODELS.ROUTING.ACCEPTANCE_DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.ACCEPTANCE_DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_SEC), [`MODELS.ROUTING.PLUGIN_PREFETCH_WINDOW_DEFAULT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.PLUGIN_PREFETCH_WINDOW_DEFAULT), or [`MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_TRUST_ENV`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_CLIENT_TRUST_ENV).

Everything under [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY) sits outside the reloadable set and does record a pending restart. [Configuration scopes and restart behavior](#configuration-scopes-and-restart-behavior) covers the reload rules for the rest of the configuration.

#### Bound what SoAI accepts

[`MODELS.ROUTING.TASK_QUEUE_MAX_SIZE`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.TASK_QUEUE_MAX_SIZE) defaults to `1000` and bounds the in-memory scheduling queue. A full queue produces an explicit refusal rather than an unbounded wait, which [Resilience and self-healing](#resilience-and-self-healing) describes. The value applies live, although shrinking it while the queue is fuller than the new limit only takes the limit down to the current occupancy and logs that it did. Keep it at 1 or above. Neither this key nor [`MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS) has a minimum in the settings schema, so a `0` saves without complaint and then fails when SoAI rebuilds the routing configuration, which makes it a way to break routing rather than a way to remove a cap.

Durable admission is checked before any of that, inside the database write that records the task. [`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS) caps non-terminal durable tasks and its factory value of `0` disables that ceiling, [`MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT) defaults to `268435456`, or 256 MiB, measured on the volume that holds the system database, and [`MODELS.ROUTING.ACCEPTANCE_DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.ACCEPTANCE_DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_SEC) gives that write 30 seconds to reach the database before acceptance fails. Set a positive durable limit when the instance needs a queue ceiling, keep the three aligned with storage and recovery capacity, and restart after changing any of them, because accepting more durable work than the instance can bring to a truthful terminal state is worse than refusing it.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_ASYNC_ACCEPT_DEFAULT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HTTP_ASYNC_ACCEPT_DEFAULT) is `false`, so an HTTP inference request holds its connection unless the client sends `Prefer: respond-async`. An asynchronous acceptance answers `202` with a body carrying the accepted status and the task id, plus a `Preference-Applied: respond-async` header, and the caller collects the result later. Turning the default on applies it to streaming requests as well and there is no header that asks for the synchronous behavior back, so it suits automation that polls and breaks a client waiting on the response body. A request that asks for its completion to be stored stays synchronous either way.

#### Limit what runs at once

| Control | Factory default | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS) | `2` | Non-persistent plugin backends resident at the same time. |
| [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_CONCURRENT_TASKS_PER_PLUGIN.DEFAULT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_CONCURRENT_TASKS_PER_PLUGIN.DEFAULT) | `4` | Running inference tasks on one plugin, for a plugin that declares no limit of its own. |
| [`MODELS.ROUTING.OWNER_RUNNING_LIMITS.DEFAULT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.OWNER_RUNNING_LIMITS.DEFAULT) | `4` | Running inference tasks for one owner unless an owner-type override applies. |

The plugin limit has a shortcut in the WebUI: open **Plugins**, select **Configure concurrent plugins** on the **Concurrent plugins** card, change **Maximum concurrent plugins**, and select **Save**. It accepts a whole number from 1 through 1000, and saving it is a configuration change like any other, so it needs the same permission. Persistent plugins do not consume the limit, and [Capacity planning](#capacity-planning) explains how SoAI looks for a safe eviction candidate when every slot is occupied.

The per-plugin task limit is the one to read carefully, because a loaded plugin that declares its own concurrency wins over the configured value, which then applies only to a plugin that declares none. Every bundled plugin declares one: 1 for [Ollama](https://ollama.com/), [MeloTTS](https://github.com/myshell-ai/MeloTTS), and [Whisper](https://github.com/openai/whisper), 2 for [CTranslate2](https://opennmt.net/CTranslate2/), 4 for Embedding and [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp), 16 for [vLLM](https://vllm.ai/), and 100 for External. Open **Plugins**, select the plugin, and read **Max concurrent** in **Plugin information** to see what a given plugin is actually enforcing.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.PROMPT_QUEUING`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.PROMPT_QUEUING) is `false` and adds a fourth cap when you turn it on, admitting at most 4 tasks at a time out of the priority queue and into scheduling. That slot count is fixed and has no configuration path, so treat the setting as on or off rather than as a number you can size.

##### Override one plugin or one owner type

Use [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_CONCURRENT_TASKS_PER_PLUGIN.PER_PLUGIN`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.MAX_CONCURRENT_TASKS_PER_PLUGIN.PER_PLUGIN) only for a measured plugin-specific difference, and only for a plugin that leaves the limit to SoAI. In Advanced settings, search for that complete path and enter a JSON object keyed by plugin name:

```json
{"my-plugin": 2}
```

An owner is the thing SoAI counts running work against, and there are four kinds: `conversation`, `http_request`, `mcp_client`, and `system`. [`MODELS.ROUTING.OWNER_RUNNING_LIMITS.PER_OWNER_TYPE`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.OWNER_RUNNING_LIMITS.PER_OWNER_TYPE) takes an object keyed by those names, so you can give API traffic a different ceiling from WebUI conversations without touching the default. A limit of `0` or less removes the check for that owner type, which is rarely what you want, since the limit exists so one account, script, or key cannot hold every running slot.

##### Size each plugin's queue

Each plugin also has its own bounded queue in front of its workers, and overflowing it refuses the dispatch rather than growing. SoAI divides [`MODELS.ROUTING.TASK_QUEUE_MAX_SIZE`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.TASK_QUEUE_MAX_SIZE) by the number of plugins to get a share, raises that share to [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_MIN_SIZE`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_MIN_SIZE), which is `16`, or to the plugin's concurrency limit multiplied by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_BURST_FACTOR`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_BURST_FACTOR), which is `4`, whichever is largest, and caps the result at the global budget. Raise the burst factor when a plugin with a small concurrency limit needs to absorb bursts, and raise the minimum size when many plugins are dividing one queue budget between them.

The worker count follows the concurrency limit rather than the queue: a plugin runs one dispatcher worker per unit of concurrency, capped by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_MAX_WORKERS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_MAX_WORKERS) at `32`, so External with its declared 100 gets 32 workers rather than 100. A plugin that declares unlimited concurrency instead gets [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_UNLIMITED_WORKERS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.PLUGIN_QUEUE_UNLIMITED_WORKERS), which is `8`.

##### Keep one busy plugin from crowding the others

[`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAIR_DISPATCH_ENABLED`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAIR_DISPATCH_ENABLED) is `true` and engages only when every plugin slot is already occupied and another plugin is waiting for capacity. While that holds, a non-persistent plugin that has reached its share stops receiving new dispatches until the waiting plugins get theirs. [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAIR_DISPATCH_MAX_PER_PLUGIN`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.FAIR_DISPATCH_MAX_PER_PLUGIN) is `32`, but the share is the lower of that ceiling and the plugin's own concurrency limit, so on a default instance the plugin limit is what binds and raising the ceiling changes nothing. Persistent plugins are never throttled this way, and turning fairness off lets the priority order run unmodified, which favors whichever plugin is already warm.

##### Plan and prefetch queued work

[`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NUM_PLANNER_WORKERS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NUM_PLANNER_WORKERS) defaults to `16` and sets how many workers pull tasks from the priority queue and turn them into scheduling decisions. The minimum is 1. Raising it helps only when planning is the bottleneck rather than the backends, and it is the one control here where the direction of the change matters.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.PLUGIN_PREFETCH_WINDOW_DEFAULT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.PLUGIN_PREFETCH_WINDOW_DEFAULT) defaults to `8` and limits how many claimed durable items SoAI keeps in memory per priority class ahead of execution. A larger window gives the scheduler more to choose from at the cost of holding more leases, and the drain loop reads it at startup along with its lease and sweep intervals, so the change lands on the next restart.

#### Set the deadlines an inference must meet

Several controls under `HEALTH_CHECKS` bound ordinary inference rather than probes, and these are the ones that decide when a slow backend produces a timeout instead of an answer.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NON_STREAMING_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.NON_STREAMING_TIMEOUT_SEC) defaults to `300.0` and bounds a non-streaming attempt. [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SEC) also defaults to `300.0` and bounds the gap between streamed chunks, so it governs a stalled stream rather than a slow one.

**The deadline for the first streamed chunk is not fixed, because a long prompt legitimately takes longer to prefill.** SoAI divides the prompt token count by [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_PREFILL_MIN_TOKENS_PER_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_PREFILL_MIN_TOKENS_PER_SEC), which is `50.0`, adds [`MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_PREFILL_OVERHEAD_SEC`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.HEALTH_CHECKS.STREAMING_PREFILL_OVERHEAD_SEC), which is `60.0`, and uses whichever is larger, that result or the non-streaming timeout. A per-request timeout from the client caps the outcome. On a host slower than 50 tokens per second of prefill, lowering the assumed rate is the correct fix for first-chunk timeouts on long prompts, rather than raising the base timeout for every request.

#### Handle disconnects and duplicate work

[`MODELS.ROUTING.CANCEL_ON_CLIENT_DISCONNECT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.CANCEL_ON_CLIENT_DISCONNECT) defaults to `false`. When it is on and a streaming client goes away, SoAI publishes a cancellation for that task, so the disconnect becomes a cancellation outcome instead of work that continues with nobody reading it. **Each stream reads the setting as it opens, so the change reaches new streams at once.** Leave it off when a caller is expected to reconnect or to collect accepted asynchronous work later, and remember that the request still ends only as fast as the selected plugin honors cancellation.

[`MODELS.ROUTING.DEDUPLICATION_ENABLED`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DEDUPLICATION_ENABLED) defaults to `true`, letting eligible identical requests share one lead execution while the rest wait on its result. Streaming requests are excluded outright. By default the match covers the request payload, the resolved execution targets, the priority, and the parameter snapshot, and [`MODELS.ROUTING.DEDUPLICATION_KEYS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DEDUPLICATION_KEYS) narrows the payload half to named fields when a field that does not affect the output keeps identical work apart. Keep ordinary admission limits either way, because deduplication reduces only duplicate work.

#### Release idle model resources

**[`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.MODELS.ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.MODELS.ENABLED) is off by default, and what SoAI counts as activity is worth knowing before you turn it on.** The monitor watches for a model load, an inference request, or an embedding request, but only the MCP paths publish those two request events, so a conversation in the WebUI and a call to the compatible API leave the timer running. On an instance whose traffic arrives that way, the clock measures time since the last model load rather than time since the last request.

When the setting is on, SoAI checks every [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.CHECK_INTERVAL_SEC`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.CHECK_INTERVAL_SEC) seconds, `15` by default, and acts once the instance has been idle for [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.MODELS.TIMEOUT_MINUTES`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.MODELS.TIMEOUT_MINUTES), which is `10`. The action is the same force stop the administrator command performs rather than a quiet unload, so it cancels running work and drains the queue, finalizing those tasks as failed with the reason that all plugins are being stopped, and only then stops the plugins. Read that together with the activity rule above and leave the setting off unless the deployment is genuinely idle between sessions or its traffic arrives over MCP.

System inactivity is a separate mechanism, also off by default, and it reads the same activity signal. [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.TIMEOUT_MINUTES`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.TIMEOUT_MINUTES) is `30`, [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.ACTION`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.ACTION) accepts `shutdown` or `unload_models`, and `shutdown` is the factory value, so enabling [`SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.ENABLED`](#config-SYSTEM.INACTIVITY.SYSTEM.ENABLED) without changing the action stops the SoAI application after 30 minutes. It stops SoAI rather than the host, which is a separate operation described in [System power and application lifecycle](#system-power-and-application-lifecycle), and recovery means starting the service again. Choosing `unload_models` runs the same force stop that model inactivity uses, and system inactivity is evaluated first, so its action replaces the model action rather than running beside it.

#### Verify a change

1. Record completed throughput, latency distribution, queue depth, rejections, plugin concurrency, memory, and provider limits.
2. Change one control, and restart only if that control needs it.
3. Repeat the same workload through steady state and recovery.
4. Keep the change only if terminal outcomes and operating margin are still acceptable.

### Capacity planning [page: capacity-planning]

Capacity planning starts from the work SoAI must finish, not from the largest queue the host can hold. Describe the models, request shapes, concurrent owners, tools, file processing, storage growth, and recovery target, then measure that workload on the host that will run it and set admission limits below the point where it stopped improving. [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning) holds the individual controls and their factory values, [Storage paths and host capacity](#storage-paths-and-host-capacity) covers where the data goes, and [Resilience and self-healing](#resilience-and-self-healing) describes what SoAI does once a limit is reached, so this page is about arriving at the numbers.

#### Describe the workload

| Input | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Inference | Model and quantization, context and output length, streaming, image or audio inputs, reasoning, and backend. |
| Demand | Concurrent users or API keys, burst size, sustained request rate, automation schedules, and acceptable wait. |
| Tools | Browser sessions, shell work, web or provider calls, subagents, mail and calendar sync, and image generation. |
| Data | Model downloads, managed files, Knowledge collections, logs, histories, backups, and expected monthly growth. |
| Recovery | Required backup frequency, restore time, update headroom, and behavior during one plugin or provider failure. |

#### Measure one representative unit

Run one request with the intended model and backend, and record model load time, time to first output, total duration, input and output tokens, peak RAM and VRAM, and storage activity. Repeat with the longest ordinary context and each media or tool path that changes resource use, because a short text prompt is not a safe proxy for a document-heavy agent turn.

For remote providers, record provider concurrency and rate limits, network latency, timeout behavior, and cost policy. **Local compute capacity does not remove a remote quota, and remote inference does not remove local agent, file, queue, or database work.**

SoAI answers part of the question before anything is downloaded. In the SoAI WebUI, open **Models**, select **Add model**, and select **Check**, which compares the selected variant's declared download size, memory, and VRAM requirements against the disk, VRAM, and combined memory it currently detects, then reports whether each one fits, whether the model is runnable on this system, and estimated download and load times. [Models catalog](#models-catalog) covers the download steps. Read the result as a fit check for one model sitting alone on an idle host, since it knows nothing about context length, concurrent requests, or the other backends you intend to keep resident.

##### Increase concurrency until a limit appears

1. Start at one running request and a small bounded queue.
2. Increase concurrent owners and requests in controlled steps.
3. Watch completed throughput, latency, queue depth, rejections, plugin state, RAM, VRAM, temperature, disk, and network.
4. Stop increasing when throughput stops improving, latency exceeds the service goal, errors rise, or recovery margin disappears.

Read completed throughput rather than queue depth, because a queue that keeps growing is evidence of the limit and not evidence of capacity. **Metrics** charts **Queue depth** beside requests, latency, and tokens, while **Hardware** shows what the host was doing at the same moment. **The ceiling belongs to the whole workload rather than to a single setting.**

#### When every plugin slot is occupied

[`MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MAX_CONCURRENT_PLUGINS) bounds how many non-persistent plugin backends stay resident, and reaching it does not refuse work on its own, because SoAI first looks for a plugin it can evict safely. A non-persistent plugin in Error or Quarantined state goes first whether or not it is busy, and after that SoAI takes an idle plugin that holds a loaded model, has no active task, has an empty plugin queue, and is in a state that can be interrupted. A model loaded within the last 30 seconds is left alone so a backend that has just paid its load cost is not evicted before it serves anything.

When no candidate exists, the task is deferred with a reason recording that the instance is at capacity, and it stays queued for the next scheduling cycle instead of failing. Plan around that, because a slot limit set too low turns into waiting and repeated model loading rather than a visible error, and the model load time you measured earlier is the price of each swap.

**Persistent plugins sit outside the count entirely, so they neither consume a slot nor become eviction candidates.** The bundled embedding, speech to text, text to speech, and external provider plugins are all persistent, which makes their memory part of the steady state on every host that keeps them enabled, and browser workers, Knowledge processing, and scheduled integrations run beside inference in the same way.

#### Turn the measurements into limits

Set the per-plugin task limit at the concurrency where the backend stopped gaining throughput rather than above it, since a backend that batches internally can get slower as external concurrency rises. Keep the owner limit low enough that one account, script, or key cannot hold every running slot while the rest of the workload waits. Size the queue from the wait a caller will tolerate rather than from what memory allows.

Durable admission is where storage meets capacity, and it runs two checks in a fixed order. [`MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.DURABLE_QUEUE_HARD_LIMIT_TASKS) is evaluated first, with its factory value of `0` leaving the count unbounded, and then [`MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT`](#config-MODELS.ROUTING.MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES_FOR_ACCEPT) refuses acceptance when the volume holding the system database has less than its 256 MiB reserve free. Set both from the storage and recovery capacity the host actually has, and treat a reserve rejection as a capacity signal rather than an obstacle to work around. [Scheduler and runtime tuning](#scheduler-and-runtime-tuning) holds each path and its factory value.

#### Plan for the degraded case

**A virtual model adds capacity across requests rather than within one.** Each request is dispatched to a single eligible member while the remaining members stay as its failover order, so more members raise throughput when several requests are in flight and do nothing for the latency of one. Test normal routing and the loss of each required member, and expect a failover target to have a lower quota, a different capability, or higher latency. Keep enough queue and timeout margin for a bounded transition, without promising that every failed request is safe to replay.

Storage is the part that fails slowly. Models, plugin runtimes, managed files, Knowledge indexes, the database, logs, retained backups, and browser data each grow at their own rate, and [Storage paths and host capacity](#storage-paths-and-host-capacity) plans their placement while [Data storage, retention, and relocation](#data-storage-retention-and-relocation) owns retention and the safe move sequence. Include the temporary space a download, extraction, update, or relocation needs, and keep a verified backup outside the host, because another directory on the same volume is not recovery capacity.

#### Set the operating boundary

Choose limits that leave memory, disk, and scheduler margin for cancellation, logging, health checks, backups, updates, and a degraded backend. **Refusing new work with an explicit capacity outcome is safer than accepting a backlog the instance cannot finish.** Revisit the numbers after changing a model, context limit, backend variant, driver, provider plan, tool selection, retention policy, or user population, and keep the workload definition and its measurements with the deployment so a later operator can tell a planned limit from a fault.

##### Deployment readiness checklist

- The normal and peak workload has a recorded test.
- Admission limits are below measured saturation.
- One member or provider can fail without making accepted work permanently ambiguous.
- Storage includes growth, update, relocation, and backup headroom.
- Backups are verified and a restore has been tested.
- Monitoring retains enough evidence to identify the limiting resource.
